title: Man Indicted on Kidnapping Charge
author: Marty Madden mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Man indicted on kidnapping charge

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 304
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An incident that led to a man's arrest in June 2024 resulted in a five-count indictment this summer from a Calvert County grand jury.The defendant is identified in court papers as Edward Dewey Viens Jr., 39, of Laurel.
According to court documents, on June 5, 2024, deputies from the county's sheriff's office were initially sent to the Huntingtown area in response to a missing person report. The deputies were then dispatched to CalvertHealth Medical Center after it was learned the 32-year-old woman who had been reported missing had been located.
Viens was also at the hospital, investigators reported.
In charging papers filed by Deputy Ryan Gough, the woman claimed she had been held against her will by Viens, who was her boyfriend at the time.
Gough said Viens' accuser had bruises on her face, lacerations on her arms, neck, hands and legs, which were the result of an alleged assault by the defendant. That assault reportedly occurred while the two were riding in Viens' truck.
Gough stated in court documents that the woman told him Viens exhibited strange behavior during the ride and kept insisting the truck was being followed. She said at one point she tried to flee the truck, which led to Viens assaulting her.
Another sheriff's officer, Detective Thomas Buckler III, confirmed Viens was making strange remarks about being followed.
A search of Viens yielded four packages of suspected Suboxone.
The July 21 indictment charges Viens with one count each of kidnapping, first-degree assault, second-degree assault, possession of contraband in a place of confinement and false imprisonment.
Viens initial circuit court appearance was Monday before Judge Andrew S. Rappaport.
A pre-trial conference is scheduled for late August with a plea hearing scheduled for late September.
Prosecution of the case will be handled by Anthony R. Navalaney of the Calvert County State's Attorney's Office.
Viens is being represented by the public defenders office.

title: Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 262

 Read News Document

 A Newark park will be closed for the foreseeable future after a recent inspection found "significant safety concerns and hazardous conditions," city officials said.One of the city's lesser-known parks, Coleman Park is located near the Maryland border, bounded by Valley Road and the Country Hills and Briarcreek neighborhoods. The main entrance is in Country Hills.
The 8.5-acre park contains walking trails but otherwise is preserved in its natural state.
The inspection found that the tree canopy near the entrance to the park consists of many black locust trees that are structurally compromised by fungal decay and pose a significant risk of falling.
The walking paths are eroded and surrounded by dense thickets of greenbrier, multiflora rose and poison ivy.
"These thorny species have overgrown the area and become entangled with large woody debris from fallen trees and limbs," City Manager Tom Coleman wrote in a memo to city council. "Significant land clearing and tree removal must be completed before we can reopen the park."
The city does not have funding for such work in the 2025 budget, according to Coleman, who did not provide any indication as to when the park might reopen.
The city's five-year capital improvement plan includes plans for broader improvements to Coleman Park, such as building a turf/meadow area, planting new trees and possibly paving the trails. However that $50,000 in funding, which is dependent on a state grant, is not budgeted until 2027.
Coleman Park was created in 1993 when Newark purchased the land for $180,000 and annexed it into the city. It is named for the family that previously owned the property.

title: Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Starting July 8, police in Delaware will use electronic speed cameras to help enforce speed limits in the Interstate 95 construction zone near Del. 896 in Newark.The first three weeks will be a warning period. After the warning period, registered vehicle owners receiving a first offense will receive a base violation of $20, plus an additional amount for each mile per hour over the posted work zone speed limit of 55 mph.
For example, if the captured violation occurs at a speed of 66 mph, the speed violation is $20 plus an additional $11, which accounts for $1 for each mile per hour over the speed limit. Additional fees and court costs that are tacked on to all speeding tickets in Delaware will bring the total cost up to $118.
Second and subsequent offenses are higher. These violations are civil penalties only, and no points will be assessed to drivers' licenses.
State officials first announced the program in April, saying the cameras are an important tool to make work zones safer.
"Even though we've reduced the speed limits out here in the work zone, we're still seeing people speeding through there," Delaware Department of Transportation Secretary Nicole Majeski said at the time. "It is a tight configuration, so law enforcement has difficulty pulling people over. We've also seen a spike in crashes, so we're hoping the cameras will help."
Similar to the red light cameras common throughout the state, speed cameras will take pictures of violators' license plates, and those drivers will receive a ticket in the mail. The driver must exceed the speed limit by at least 11 mph in order to receive a ticket via a speed camera.
DelDOT first used speed cameras in 2022 when the state legislature authorized a pilot program focused on an I-95 project in Wilmington.
"We saw speeds reduced significantly, both northbound and southbound, and accidents were cut in half," Majeski said. "We saw as a direct result of having those cameras that people slow down, and it really paid off."
Last year, after lobbying from Newark officials and others, the legislature expanded the program to allow cameras in work zones and residential areas throughout the state. After developing regulations and choosing a vendor, DelDOT is ready to install the first new cameras in the work zone at the I-95/Del. 896 interchange, which is in the midst of a two-year reconstruction project.
Brandon Zerilla, who is leading the project for DelDOT contractor Wagman, said earlier this year that the cameras will be a welcomed safety tool for his workers.
"These cameras have proven to reduce the speeds in the work zone, reduce crashes and increase awareness in the work zone," Zerilla said, adding that far too many drivers do not slow down while passing through the I-95 construction site.
The interchange project, which is the largest work zone in Delaware, involves building new flyover ramps from southbound Del. 896 to northbound I-95 and from southbound I-95 to southbound Del. 896. The flyovers will increase the distance between exit and entrance ramps, reducing the traffic weaving that causes crashes at the current interchange.
The project also includes widening a one-mile stretch of the interstate to provide for longer acceleration and deceleration lanes, as well as upgraded lighting, rehabilitation of 10 existing bridges, the construction of six new bridges for the flyovers, and the construction of a walking and biking bridge over the interstate.
Work began last spring and will continue through fall 2025.

Police nab theft suspects who allegedly stole $8K in perfume from Ulta store

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News

 Five out-of-state individuals — four men and a woman — have been charged with felony theft following an alleged theft of nearly $8,000 worth of merchandise from Ulta Beauty in Prince Frederick.The incident occurred on April 4 at approximately 4:37 p.m., according to the Calvert County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to the store when a call went out that a theft had occurred.
According to a sheriff's office report, "Two males and one female entered the store and placed numerous colognes and perfumes into bags and fled the store. After fleeing the store, witnesses observed all three suspects enter a gray Mercury Montego that fled northbound on Route 4."
According to court documents filed by Deputy Antonio Tavares, Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the Mercury traveling northbound on Route 4, which then turned onto Route 2.
MacWilliams "initiated a traffic stop in the area of Pushaw Station Road in Sunderland. During the traffic stop, five occupants were located in the suspect vehicle along with numerous bags of perfumes and colognes in plain view. The total value of the stolen items was approximately $7,694 dollars."
In addition to the merchandise that was allegedly stolen from the Prince Frederick store, Tavares reported in charging papers that several cellphones were also confiscated.
The five arrested are identified as Yeiner Jose Rodriguez Barcelo, 27, of Bronx, N.Y., Yoncar Alberto Rainoso, 21, of Manhattan, N.Y., Estefani Andrea Urbano-Zapata, 21, of Cape Girardea, Mo., Raimil Marquez Jimenez, 25, of Washington, D.C., and Adony Josue Carana, 27, of Manhattan N.Y.
A sheriff's office press release stated that further investigation revealed Rodriguez-Barcelo was wanted on an open warrant from Pennsylvania for felony retail theft related to thefts at Ulta stores in Pennsylvania.
Court records show Carana, who was also listed with the alias Carrano, has been released after posting $10,000 bond. As of Monday, the other four remained at the Calvert detention center on a no-bond status.
A district court hearing on the charges the five are facing is scheduled for June 3. Language interpreters have been requested for four of the five defendants, court records show.
The Prince Frederick Ulta has been the scene of similar thefts over the last three years. Other Ulta stores regionally and nationally have been targets of alleged thieves. Several national news outlets have reported allegations of a possible retail theft ring in the state of California. The alleged perpetrators there stole $8 million in cosmetics from several chains, including Ulta, and then sold the products on Amazon.
It is not known at this time if the five arrested in Calvert last week are part of a larger theft ring.
Calvert County Sheriff Ricky Cox (R) issued a note of thanks in an agency press release to "the witnesses on scene that went above and beyond to promptly call 911 and provide details of the suspects and suspects' vehicle. Your efforts are greatly appreciated."

title: Snow Fall Brings Snow Day on the Eastern Shore
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Snow fall brings snow day on the Eastern Shore

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 EASTON — Residents woke up to two inches of snow Tuesday morning in Easton.With the snow came a snow day for Talbot County Public Schools students. Weather conditions caused the school system to close for the entire day.
Dorchester County Public Schools also closed for the day due to icy road conditions. Caroline County Public Schools closed for students, but offices opened at 10 a.m. for its 12-month employees.
Easton's Superintendent of Public Works Mike Dickerson said Easton Public Works used 46.92 tons of salt to keep the town's roadways safe. He said the department applied salt to the town's main roads — roads like Washington Street that get you into town — three times.
After receiving a notification from the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services, Easton Public Works began salting roads at 4 p.m. Monday. Dickerson said the last of the department's five trucks finished salting for the third time at 4:44 a.m. on Tuesday.
"We had five trucks out," he said. "And each one of them has an assigned route."
According to the National Weather Service, winter weather advisories for Queen Anne's, Talbot and Caroline counties were issued early Tuesday morning and in effect until 1 p.m. on Tuesday.
The advisories were for mixed precipitation with additional snow of up to an inch and ice accumulation of around one 10th of an inch. The advisories stated that morning commutes could be affected due to slippery road conditions.
Dorchester County received a winter weather advisory from the National Weather Service for freezing rain and additional ice accumulation. The advisory was in effect until 11 a.m. Tuesday morning.
As of noon on Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service, snow and freezing rain were likely in Easton before 1 p.m. with a chance of rain and snow between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. and a chance of more snow after 2 p.m. Little or no snow accumulation is expected. A tenth of an inch of ice accumulation is possible.
Dickerson said Easton Public Works has its trucks prepared in the event that employees have to go back out to take care of the roads.

 On July 21, Baltimore City police, first responders and outreach workers went in full force to clear out the homeless encampment at the corner of Dundalk and Holabird Avenues.A "No Trespassing" notice was posted earlier this month, stating that the area would be cleared on July 21.The Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services and nonprofit groups visited the site before it was cleared to connect people with resources like shelter and drug treatment. The area was cleared by noon."Members of the Baltimore County Homeless Services Division have been working closely with Baltimore City officials to address the encampment near Dundalk and Holabird Avenues," Baltimore City police said in a statement sent to the Old Dundalk Neighborhood Association. "We understand how concerning it is to see this situation in your community. People began living in tents on a strip of grass in front of the Holabird Business Park earlier this year.Community groups wrote to county and city leaders for months asking for a solution, but the encampment was located just inside the city line. In February, they wrote a letter to officials to request a solution.People living in tents longterm poses a lot of public health concerns, and city police were regularly called out to the encampment.Several people in the camp used drugs during the daytime, and panhandling at the intersection was very common.Baltimore police Precinct 12 Capt. title: 'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — On Sundays, when the pews should have been packed, the Rev. Dennis Morgan would walk into St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Vienna and, at most, see two parishioners prepared for sermon.That is until Sept. 21, when the parish had its final service and St. Paul's closed its doors for good. The church's closure was not the town's first this year.
St. Paul's was deconsecrated just months after Vienna United Methodist Church, located directly across the street, stopped its services, Morgan said.
"It's a very, very bittersweet time," he said. "You know, realizing that it must be done, but, at the same time, you know, it's heartbreaking."
The church closures are the consequence of attendance trends seen in Vienna and across the country.
About 33% of adults in the United States attend religious services in person as of February 2025. This is a dramatic decline from 2007, when 50% of adults attended religious services in person, according to a recent Pew Research Center study.
"There have been really low numbers at St. Paul's for several years, and it just wasn't sustainable," said Administrative Assistant to the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton Lynn Anstatt.
In 2020, there were 18 parishioners on the books at St. Paul's, with roughly eight members attending services weekly. This dropped to 11 members on the books with around two attending weekly services by 2025, Morgan said.
He said the pandemic and static population of Vienna largely contributed to decreased attendance of all the churches in the area. Only a handful still hold weekly services.
Keeping St. Paul's open and active had become an existential question for Morgan.
"We could have kept the property going probably for quite a while, but we had no mission, no outreach and we questioned the 'why' of it more than the 'how' of it," the pastor said.
Morgan was in conversation with the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton for around three years in an attempt to keep the church open. But after seeing minimal improvement, he could no longer justify keeping the parish going.
"The church is still available to use although it has been deconsecrated, so we do have access to the church. But in terms of services and everything, that does come to an end," Morgan said.
The decommissioning of St. Paul's comes after more than 300 years of active service in Vienna.
There are now no Episcopal Churches in Vienna, but because attendance was so low and the church was not involved in the community, Morgan doesn't think the deconsecration will have much negative impact on the larger Vienna community.
Many community members have family buried in the cemetery on the property and have inquired with Morgan about the cemetery's future.
"The difficult decision to close the church, despite such a vast legacy, was driven by factors such as declining membership and the increasing costs of maintaining historic structures," former parishioner of St. Paul's and Vienna resident Susan Donaghue wrote in an email to the Star Democrat. "The conclusion of ministry at St. Paul's marks the end of an era for the town of Vienna and the community it so faithfully served."

title: Hornberger to Introduce Citizenship Check for Voters
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Hornberger to introduce citizenship check for voters

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: State News 
 
 306

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Cecil County Del. Kevin Hornberger (R) says he likely has bipartisan support for a resolution he plans to bring before the Maryland General Assembly in January that would require the Maryland State Board of Elections to verify the citizenship of every registered voter in Maryland."Virginia and Colorado — both fairly 'blue' states — are already doing this," Hornberger said. "So I say, 'Hey, State of Maryland, you need to participate in this program.'"
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlement program is an online service that verifies a benefit or license applicant's immigration status for US citizenship. It does likewise for those who are naturalized, acquired or US born, giving this information to agencies to assure only those allowed get these entitlements. That includes the right to vote, Hornberger said.
"This tells the Board of Elections to participate," Hornberger said. "I think we'll have bipartisan support."
Party affiliation is not the issue, Hornberger said, even though Democrats told Republican members of the General Assembly that this was unnecessary. "They said you guys are offering solutions to a problem that doesn't exist. Well, guess what?"
The recent arrest of an Iowa public schools superintendent — who previously resided in Maryland — is what made Hornberger pursue the SAVE Act legislation.
"He was in this country illegally and he was registered as a Democrat in Maryland," he said.
Calling Maryland "one of the largest immigration states in the country," Hornberger said the SAVE Act wouldn't carry any penalties.
"It's just saying they can't vote," he said. If the resolution gets approved, Hornberger said it would make elections fair. "Every board in Maryland would have to use the federal voter registry database to assure that everyone registered to vote in the state of Maryland are legally residents."
The bill would first go before the House Ways and Means Committee, of which Hornberger is a member.

title: Data Center Pause Underscores Local Concerns About Widespread Impacts
author: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service
content:
Data center pause underscores local concerns about widespread impacts

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 958
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — A proposed data center project in Prince George's County, Maryland, was paused on Sept. 16 to give a task force time to evaluate potential impacts on public health, the environment and energy demand.The Prince George's project is controversial, underscoring growing public concerns over the proliferation of data centers nationwide.
Data centers can range from massive warehouse-sized facilities to office buildings and are the physical backbone of everything digital.
The growth of these centers has surged, with 44 operational or planned data centers in Maryland, according to Data Center Map. Prince George's County is one of the latest battlegrounds where local opposition has slowed what data center supporters insist would be a major boom to the economy.
"The only reason the county is considering data centers is for money," Prince George's County Council Member Wala Blegay said in an interview with Capital News Service. "The reality is that our commercial tax base is very low. We're mostly relying on residential (taxes) because our residents are not able to get relief on the high property taxes that we have here. That is why we are looking at data centers."
Blegay's District 6 borders the District of Columbia and is mostly inside the Capital Beltway, encompassing communities including Suitland, District Heights, Marlow Heights, Camp Springs and Forestville.
The county council created the Qualified Data Center Task Force in April 2025. The council faced local protests at their three meetings in July from residents concerned about energy consumption, electric bills and environmental factors.
On Sept. 16, the council approved a resolution pausing the development of current and future data center projects until the task force has completed its work. The task force is expected to release its findings in November.
"There is no point in having a task force if all of these projects can move forward," Blegay said. "We're studying all of these infrastructure issues. So we're talking about the next three months, we're going to be passing legislation to address that… and we don't want people to rush out and expedite their process, so they'll get ahead of us."
Prince George's County Executive Aisha Braveboy told Washington's WTOP radio that the county council's 2021 decision to speed up the data center approval process "was a huge mistake because the residents have a stake in where these data centers are located."
"I'm in support generally of data centers," Braveboy said. "I do believe it's a really good economic tool in the right locations."
"I think we gotta look at what the land use implications are and be really thorough in these decisions," Del. Ashanti F. Martinez, D-Prince George's, said in a Sept. 18 Instagram post. "You know, at the state level we try to provide as much oversight as possible, and I'm really concerned that we are moving a little fast on the data center conversation."
Access to electricity and the price residents pay are critics' primary concerns, as the average monthly electric bill for Maryland, according to poweroutage.us, stands at $167.55. Electric bills are expected to slightly rise with the anticipated new data centers, according to a letter from the Office of People's Council for the State of Maryland.
"What we know is that no data center is going to be turned on, especially with high gigawatts, not within the next four to five years, because of all the issues with electricity and energy sourcing," Blegay said.
Maryland currently does not produce enough electricity on its own, so it relies on importing the shortfall from outside the state.
"Historically, Maryland has imported about 40% of its annual electric needs from other states," according to a 2024 fact sheet from PJM, a transmission organization that coordinates the use of wholesale electricity among 13 states and the District of Columbia.
As of last year, data centers accounted for about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption, according to a report from the Department of Energy (DOE).
"(AI is) a much more significant data hog than any type of search you have today, and it's something that is exponentially growing with the types of searches Americans are doing," Michael Kratsios, director of the White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy, told a Sept. 10 hearing of the Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation Committee's science, manufacturing, and competitiveness.
The increased use of AI has provided an opening for Republicans who advocate a renewed reliance on traditional fuels to meet the energy demand. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, for example, wants "good, old-fashioned" coal and gas to provide U.S. power needs.
"When you had 94% of new power generation in America over the last four years, be it wind and solar, that probably isn't nearly enough to produce the kind of energy that we need to power the AI revolution," Moreno said at the subcommittee hearing.
But Sen. Edward Markey, D-Massachusetts, warned that "Americans' electricity bills are going to rise by as much as 25% over the next four years — 25% because of data center demand. It's not just a future fear, it's a present problem."
"So, Mr. Kratsios, do you think it's appropriate that the administration is forcing Americans to pay more on their electricity bills while using their taxpayer dollars to make the problem even worse by funding the unfettered growth of the AI industry?" Markey asked.
"I do not believe there's been an administration in American history more committed to growing power generation for the American people and lowering energy costs for everyday Americans," Kratsios responded. "And I'm proud to work for a president and administration that has that level of commitment."
In October, PG County will host another public council meeting to continue discussions about the data center. By the end of November, the Prince George's County Qualified Data Center Task Force will report its findings, giving the council six months to decide on next steps, according to the resolution.

title: Eye of the Storm: Communities Still Rebuilding and Recovering After Hurricane Helene
author: Mike Sunnucks Adams MultiMedia
content:
Eye of the storm: Communities still rebuilding and recovering after Hurricane Helene

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks Adams MultiMedia | Section: News 
 
 1182

 Read News Document

 A year ago, Hurricane Helene rampaged through Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas and Tennessee with high winds, biblical rains and destructive storm surges and floods that left 252 people dead and caused an estimated $79 billion in damage.A few weeks later, Hurricane Milton slammed Florida and Georgia, killing 46 people and causing another $34 billion in damage.
Helene brought torrential rains and deadly floods to areas of the Carolinas and Appalachia, with warmer ocean water fueling larger and more destructive hurricanes.
Some areas saw historic amounts of rain and major power outages from Helene's monstrous storm clouds.
Parts of Transylvania and Yancey counties in North Carolina were hit with 30 inches of rain. Greenville, South Carolina, saw 21.66 inches.
Heavy rains stretched from Florida to Ohio and Indiana, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
From Western Carolina and Appalachia to Florida's Gulf coast and southern Georgia, communities are still healing and rebuilding from last year's devastating hurricane season.
Those on the frontlines of the recovery efforts say progress has been made, but more work and challenges remain.
'NEARLY EVERY STRUCTURE'On Florida's Gulf coast, Hurricane Helene brought historic storm surges and flooding to the southwestern parts of the state as well as the Big Bend and Tampa Bay areas.
Some of those same areas were hit in October by Hurricane Milton.
"We had widespread flooding during Helene, with nearly every structure in the city taking water, some as much as 5 feet. Milton tore off roofs from condos and knocked down trees and power poles, many residents were without power and water for 7 to 10 days," said Trip Barrs, fire chief in the beach town of Treasure Island in the Tampa-St. Petersburg area.
Other parts of Florida also got hit by both hurricanes.
"Helene impacted some of our coastal areas on Sept. 26 last year, and then Hurricane Milton impacted a much broader area of Lee County mere days later on Oct. 9," said Betsy Clayton, communications director for Lee County, which includes Fort Myers.
That area of southwest Florida experienced a storm surge of more than 5 feet and 6 inches of rain in a short period from Hurricane Helene.
A few weeks later, Milton brought winds of 120 miles per hour, a 6.8-inch storm surge in Lee County and heavy rains. Parts of Florida saw numerous tornadoes.
Lee County collected more than 627,000 cubic yards of debris from the two storms, according to a post-storm analysis.
In Treasure Island, Barrs said roughly a year later that there are "many vacant residential and commercial lots" from the storms.
"We are starting to see some rebuilding and some homes being elevated. Many businesses were not able to reopen, and others are still in temporary facilities," he said.
Other challenges persist.
"Many residents are still not able to rebuild or repair their homes. This is due to a variety of issues: insurance, permitting, old/non-flood compliant structures. Many of our smaller, 1-story hotels will not be able to reopen," Barrs said.
High insurance costs and sometimes delayed, disputed or denied storm claims have been causes for frustrations in Florida, in particular, as well as other states.
Barrs said some hotel rooms have started to come back online, and a beach renourishment project replacing sand lost to the storm surges is slated to start "in the coming months."
Other communities and tourist attractions in Helene's path have also reopened and have been marketing and advertising that to targeted audiences.
That includes Asheville, the popular arts and tourism hub in western North Carolina.
"We're shouting it from our beautiful Blue Ridge mountaintops—the Asheville area is open for business and eagerly welcoming visitors after Hurricane Helene impacted our region in fall of 2024," said Dodie Stephens, vice president of marketing for the Explore Asheville tourism group, earlier this summer.
The group has been advertising in regional drive markets as well as cities with flight connections to Asheville.
"Downtown Asheville was largely unimpacted by the storm last fall and many of the most iconic hikes, overlooks and attractions along the Blue Ridge Parkway are open," she said.
The Biltmore gardens reopened in November 2024 and is hosting an exhibition featuring Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamum through Jan. 4, 2026.
Some areas of the Appalachian Trail damaged by Hurricane Helene have been repaired or reopened. But there continues to be repair work and debris collections in other trail areas in North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia, according to the National Park Service.
There are detour areas along the 2,200-mile trail because of storm damage and remediation.
Some Florida communities saw backlogs and delays with permitting approval after the storms.
That prompted Treasure Island and other localities to take fresh looks at its emergency planning and response, Barrs said.
In Lee County, local officials have been reexamining their communications and social media policies on how to keep the public best informed during major storms and other emergencies.
'HISTORIC DAMAGE'Beyond its coastal impacts, Helene brought major flooding, downed trees and damaged homes, buildings and roadways in Georgia, the Carolinas and Tennessee.
"At one point during the storm, over 1.2 million gallons of water per second flowed over the Nolichucky Dam. In comparison, Niagara Falls' peak daily flow is 700,000 gallons of water per second," said Mark Nagi, regional communications officer for the Tennessee Department of Transportation.
The state also removed more than 720,000 cubic yards of debris from Helene.
"This storm has caused historic damage to bridges and roadways, especially in Upper East Tennessee. TDOT anticipates hundreds of millions of dollars in damage," Nagi said.
Helene's biblical rains and floods damaged and shut down parts of Interstate 40 near the Tennessee, North Carolina border and 49 sections of state and local roadways in the eastern part of Tennessee last year, according to
"Work on full restoration of I-40 in Cocke County continues," Nagi said. "We anticipate the roadway being fully back open in Summer 2026. We have had one lane open in each direction since late October 2024."
Forty-seven of the 49 impacted state and local roadway areas have reopened, with the two remaining areas under contract to be repaired this fall and next spring.
Tennessee surveyors inspected all 490 state-owned bridges that the storm could have damaged.
Nagi said two bridges in Greene and Washington counties were built in a faster "Progressive Design-Build" mode that allowed design and construction phases to overlap.
"Those bridges were each opened in less than 8 months. Without PDB being utilized, it would have probably taken approximately 2 to 3 years to reconnect those communities," he said.
On Sept. 15, North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein called for an additional $13.5 billion in federal funding to help with Hurricane Helene reconstruction.
That includes $8 billion to help rebuild homes and small businesses, $2 billion for local governments financially strained by the storm and its cleanup, and $2 billion to help with reconstruction and full reopening of sections of I-40 hit by the storm.
Stein, a Democrat, also wants Congress to release another $10 billion in previously allocated funds related to hurricane recovery.
"Western North Carolinians are counting on the federal government for help to rebuild homes, support small businesses, and repair roads. I call on Congress to deliver for western North Carolina its fair share and appropriate an additional $13.5 billion in funding for Helene recovery," Stein said in a statement.

title: Concerns Over Data Centers Voiced at Public Meeting
author: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com
content:
Concerns over data centers voiced at public meeting

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 792
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Shouts against data centers were heard from the back of the room during a meeting earlier this month that addressed noise, water and electricity impacts but also stressed potential economic benefits.There is interest in building data centers in Charles County, Jim Chandler, director of economic development for county government, said during the Sept. 20 meeting at Mary B. Neal Elementary School.
There is a 432-acre proposed data center development located on Billingsley Road near the county landfill and recycling center, according to a presentation from NAI Michael.
Charles County is aware of the commercial development interest in the Piney Reach property for a data center, according to a statement from county government sent to Southern Maryland News.
Prince George's County had a protest against data centers because there are concerns about water, electricity and electronic waste, Carlos Childs, a Waldorf resident, said. The Charles County work group for data centers should also include members of the public and surrounding neighborhoods to provide insight, he said.
"They're saying that the Charles County government is supportive of a data center coming here," Childs said. "Which is weird that it wasn't said … or that they even mentioned the Piney Reach [data center] at all."
Childs was told about the proposed Piney Reach center and found the presentation on Google, he said.
So far, the county has not received any development plan submissions. The economic development department views this property "as an opportunity site for a number of industrial-type uses, one of which could be the future use of data centers."
"Data centers need to be carefully located and need regulation," Chandler said.
Phones, computers and GPS systems use data centers, Mark Thompson, chief of commercial development for Charles County, said. Data centers are large, one- to two-story buildings that have computer servers. They have high security to protect information and back up generators.
"For the longest time, you've heard people talking about the cloud … data centers are effectively the cloud," Thompson said.
Water impacts
Data centers require a lot of energy and get extremely hot, making the water use high to cool the systems, Thompson said. They use a closed-loop system, which keeps water in the system.
"We need to look at those things and think about them relative to other commercial uses," Thompson said.
Treated waste water is already being used for cooling at the CPV St. Charles Energy Station, which can be used for the same purpose as data centers, Jason Groth, director of planning and growth management, said.
"Our reclaimed, effluent water is ever-growing," Groth said. "As we grow, as new connections are made to the system, more water is produced. Therefore more reclaimed water is produced."
Economic benefits
Data centers can generate up to 5,000 construction jobs, and data center employees earn around $100,000 a year and generate billions of dollars in state and local taxes, Chandler said.
Data centers offer jobs for engineers, computer technicians, systems maintenance and security, Thompson said, as well as electricians, carpenters and plumbers while the center is being built.
Data centers also have a higher assessed value than homes and generate significant property taxes, Thompson said. The land sold for a data center in Frederick County generated $50 million in recreation taxes.
"That's a significant, significant revenue," Thompson said. "As we are all faced with revenue challenges throughout the state and the counties, we need to be thinking about that as a very important consideration."
The advocacy group Strong Towns Charles County is concerned about being able to support the infrastructure and impacts to wildlife, Maddie Kaba, co-leader of Strong Towns, said.
"We're talking about an initial construction boom now and all the revenue that it's going to bring in, but how are we being responsible with that money and making sure we save some of it," Kaba said.
Traffic, noise addressedData centers don't generate a lot of traffic because there are not a lot of people coming in and out, Thompson said. Cooling centers and generators generate around the same amount of noise as power plants and recycling centers.
Back up generators have to be run every 10 to 15 minutes and create noise, Groth said. To ease the noise, the generators will be built within the data center campus between two buildings.
"The further the building can be set back away from a property line or adjacent use is really key," Groth said.
While data centers should not be compared to the recycling center because it gets rid of harmful plastics and metals, Shelly Posey, a resident who lives outside La Plata, said she liked the idea of using wastewater.
"I won't say that I'm positive, but I'm in the middle," Posey said.
The county is working on a zoning text amendment that will include constraints on data centers if they were were to be built, Groth said. It will move through the public process starting in October.

 Washington — The Trump administration on Friday warned Maryland officials not to award contracts based on sex and race in the reconstruction of Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge."Any reliance on race- or sex-conscious factors in contracting decisions could introduce significant legal vulnerabilities and inefficiencies in the management of the project," Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a letter to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on Friday.
The secretary criticized the project's work plan, arguing that Moore has "prioritized race and gender-based requirements ahead of project completion."
Democrats in the Maryland congressional delegation responded in a joint statement, noting the bridge project was approved by Congress.
"As we have with other major infrastructure disasters with nationwide implications, Congress came together on a bipartisan basis to provide the full resources necessary for reconstruction to ensure it can be rebuilt as quickly and efficiently as possible," the lawmakers said.
"The federal government's commitment to fund the rebuild is enacted into law, and the construction contract was awarded through a legal, competitive, transparent process," they added.
Moore did not address Duffy's comments about sex and race.
"We will continue to work with the Trump Administration to find ways to reduce costs and rebuild faster," Moore said in a statement. "The safety of the bridge and the sound stewardship of taxpayer dollars remain our top priority as we work to fully restore economic vitality — not only to the Port of Baltimore and the State of Maryland, but for the people across the country."
Along with concerns over hiring practices, Duffy questioned the reconstruction project's budget.
"DEI contracting practices and ballooning project costs are already threatening to delay this critical project," Duffy said. "We will leverage our oversight authorities to ensure this vital bridge is rebuilt the right way."
President Donald Trump last month said on social media he might have to "rethink" federal support for the Key Bridge. He called Baltimore "crime ridden" and "out of control" and has threatened to send federal troops into the city, as he has in Los Angeles, Washington and Memphis.
Trump's warning about the bridge funds followed Moore's invitation to Trump to visit Baltimore or "keep our name out of your mouth."
The bridge collapsed in March 2024 after it was struck by a ship. The demolition of the bridge began in July. Following reconstruction, the bridge is slated to open in the fall of 2028.

title: Chair of honor: Delaware Rotary honors POWs, MIA soldiers.
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com

Chair of honor: Delaware Rotary honors POWs, MIA soldiers.

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 537

 A new display outside of city hall ensures that prisoners of war and service members still missing in action will never be forgotten in Newark, Delaware.The Newark Morning Rotary Club unveiled a POW/MIA Chair of Honor during a brief ceremony Thursday evening, on the eve of National POW/MIA Recognition Day.
"The Chair of Honor will surely stand as a testament to our commitment to remembering and respecting the courage and dedication of the brave individuals who we honor today," club president Jamie Zingaro said. "It also reminds us of the horrors of war and the tremendous impact war has on our families. As Rotarians, we recognize the importance of service above self, and this memorial will continue to remind us of the service and sacrifices so many have made to keep us free."
Hundreds of POW/MIA Chairs of Honor can be found in public spaces around the country, ranging from professional sports stadiums to city halls, and even the U.S. Capitol Building. The perpetually empty chair is meant to help people remember that even though the soldiers are not here, there's always a place for them.
Newark already has a Chair of Honor that is used at the annual Memorial Day ceremony and displayed inside city hall. However, the new one is suitable for outdoor display.
The chair was installed in an area of the city hall parking lot that also includes flagpoles and a plaque honoring city employees who served in the military. It is surrounded by stanchions topped with symbols representing each of the branches of the military, and a bronze plaque explains the purpose of the chair and includes the words "You are not forgotten."
With the blessing of city council, the Rotary Club funded the project and committed to maintaining the display in the future.
Rosely Robinson, who has helped install dozens of Chairs of Honor throughout Delaware and surrounding states, noted that since World War II, there are still 81,000 service members unaccounted for.
"Outside of their families and friends, they have nearly been forgotten," Robinson said. "This chair serves as a constant reminder of those still missing and that we have a place for them when they come home."
Of those missing, 121 are from Delaware.
"It doesn't sound like a big number, but 121 families, brothers, sisters, moms and dads are still waiting, and they should never be forgotten," Robinson said.
Ralph Galati, an Air Force captain whose plane was shot down over North Vietnam, was a prisoner of war for 14 months.
"It was not heroic. It was not brave," Galati said. "But it was performing one's duty, hopefully with dignity and to be able to return with honor."
He said he and his fellow prisoners showed their resolve through resistance by having church services, singing the national anthem and reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
"All of them were forbidden to be discussed and performed during captivity," he said. "Yet they were the very things that mattered the most to us, so we proudly recited them, regardless of the punishment or consequences. And today, none of these are taken lightly by me. It could be a flag flying gently overhead, or a song before a baseball game or a great rendition of the national anthem, the impact is still the same."

title: New Life for Boarded Up, Vacant Historic Maryland Mansion?
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
New life for boarded up, vacant historic Maryland mansion?

 July 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 828
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It has spent time as offices, non-profits and a Christian school, but Holly Hall, the Elkton mansion that sits next door to Big Elk Mall along South Bridge Street, has been boarded up and vacant for years.That is expected to change, however, according to Elkton Mayor Rob Alt. The town bought the property for $200,000 with the goal of first stabilizing it, then restoring it and repurposing it to give it a new life.
"This could be a fantastic culinary school," Alt said of the future of the home built in 1810, with an addition some 40- to 50-years later according to the Maryland Historic Trust. Even though it is deeded as a historic property, Alt said a wing identical to the one added could be built on the opposite side of the Federal style mansion. He said that would allow for construction of a commercial kitchen.
Elkton bought the property from the Cordish Company, which also owns the adjacent Big Elk Mall. As part of the purchase, David Cordish wanted assurances that the property would not be retail that would compete with stores in the shopping center.
"He thought this would be a good police station or municipal offices," Alt said.
Whatever the future holds, Alt said, the now is to get the structure stabilized. The building has been struck by fire three times, leaving the roof in a shambles.
"The number one point is to preserve and stabilize this building and bring it back to the way we knew it 30 years ago," Alt said. "It's truly going to be a passionate project for me."
Local historyAccording to paperwork filed to support Holly Hall's protection by the Maryland Historic Trust, the land was initially owned by Robert Alexander in colonial times. As British rule became stronger and the fight for freedom was beginning, Alexander sided with the Tories and left for Britain. His land was seized and a good portion of it bought at auction by Tobias Rudulph. In his will written in 1787, Rudulph left the land to his daughter. Anne Marie Rudulph married James Sewell in 1809 and Holly Hall was built the following year.
Sewell was very active in Elkton and across Maryland. He was named a commissioner by the Maryland Legislature, in charge of paving Elkton's streets in 1808. Sewell also served on a committee charged with detailing the meets and bounds of the town. By 1811, he had been named the first president of The Elkton Bank, but 1813 found him in command of troops at Fort Defiance, defending Elkton from British invasion.
Sewell later served as Cecil County Circuit Court Clerk from 1816 to 1840 and was also one of the founders of Trinity Episcopal Church in 1832. Sewell died in 1852 and was buried on the family property in a vault with an iron door. His children sold the property to Edward Wilmer in 1858, with the caveat that the family burial vault be left untouched.
The Rector of Trinity Episcopal Church during the Civil War was W.H.B. Mitchell. A horse and carriage from James E. Barroll, who owned Holly Hall by that time, was sent to the church to arrest Mitchell for treason. Union troops passed Holly Hall en route to detention. This was where Mrs. Barroll ran from the mansion and pleaded with the soldiers to allow for the use of her personal carriage to transport the rector, who was still in his robes. They agreed.
Alt remembers touring the mansion several times and recalls a concrete tunnel underneath, compete with shackles attached to the walls, leading to Big Elk Creek.
"I figure that was where they hid slaves for transport," Alt said.
One story he's heard about the history of Holly Hall can't be verified, but Alt insists its a great story regardless. One of Sewell's sons fought for the other side, Alt said. When he came home from the war his father refused him entrance to the family home.
"He died in the front yard," Alt said, adding perhaps that son still lingers there.
What's nextAlt said that, along with getting the building stabilized, he wants to improve the outward appearance.
"It's an eyesore and it sits right at the entrance to town," Alt said. Landscaping will take care of all the overgrowth attached to the brick walls. Some trees on the property would also be removed.
"I want to put up a 'Welcome to Elkton' sign," he said, envisioning one of those digital display signs that could also be used to make residents and visitors aware of upcoming events, meetings, road closures and other vital information. "It would be 100% for the community. No advertising."
With no way to estimate the cost this early in the conversation, Alt is certain Elkton will be able to get help.
"We won't use any taxpayer money," he said. "We'll do it all with grants and donations. I strongly believe we'll be able to get 75- to 80% funding through grants."
"We want to get this up and running as quickly as we can," Alt said.

title: Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 City officials in Newark, Delaware are in the early stages of evaluating whether a transitional housing village of small cabins could be a solution to local homelessness.Council members John Suchanec and Corinth Ford visited such a village in Georgetown, Delaware and suggested that a similar idea could be implemented here.
"We truly felt the experience was transformative," Suchanec said. "The approach that Georgetown has taken is starting to shape up to be a model for how you would deal with homeless sheltering."
Georgetown's Pallet Village was built in 2023 by the nonprofit Springboard Delaware. It consists of 40 small one-bedroom cabins, as well as shared bathhouses. It's become known as the Pallet Village because the cabins are produced by a company called Pallet.
"Our goal is to get unsheltered people out of the woods, get the help they need and move on to permanent housing or some form of self-independence," said Judson Malone, executive director of Springboard Delaware.
Malone said there are many reasons that people stay in the woods rather than go into traditional homeless shelters. Maybe they don't feel safe in a group shelter, they can't be with their partner, they can't bring their pet or they can't bring all their possessions.
"The most impactful thing you will do for them immediately is a lockable door with heat and air conditioning in a secure community, and that's exactly what we provided," Malone said. "Within two weeks, you'll see a difference in their demeanor simply because of the trauma that they experienced in the woods."
The Pallet Village does not require residents to be sober.
"We do not allow substance use on site, but best practices have shown that when people are in a safe space where they're accepted as they are, they can then begin to process the other issues in their life, including deciding whether or not to get treatment," Malone said. "We have a very high success rate of people voluntarily choosing to go to treatment."
Within a week of opening, the Georgetown shelter was 100 percent occupied and has remained so.
"People see a value in being there," Malone said. "They want to be there, and they want to get help and support."
Springboard Delaware works with 30 different support organizations to provide medical, mental heath, banking, employment and other services to people living at the Pallet Village.
"While people are unsheltered and in the woods, they almost never want those services," Malone said. "They really don't care about getting clean or sober, because getting high is how they survive a traumatic life."
The average length of stay is approximately three months, and then many residents of the Pallet Village move on to more permanent housing.
The Pallet Village cost approximately $1.5 million to build, money that came from the American Rescue Plan Act. Ongoing funds for operation has been harder to come by, however. Last year, Springboard Delaware had to lay off staff when a grant fell through and leaders were scrambling to piece together state money and private grants to keep the village open, according to reporting from Spotlight Delaware.
Malone said he is still working with the state to develop sustainable longterm funding.
Springboard Delaware has another $1.4 million in ARPA money to build a second Pallet Village somewhere else in the state.
"We've got the money in hand to do it," Malone said. "We just need a location."
If a Pallet Village were built in Newark, it would not require funding from the city, Malone said.
Ultimately, Springboard Delaware envisions building five to seven Pallet Villages around the state by the end of the decade.
"We have a vision, and we believe that homelessness is solvable," Malone said. "This is not the whole solution, but it's a huge part of it."
During a city council meeting last month, several council members expressed skepticism.
"Obviously, we all want to be compassionate, we all want to be empathetic, and we all want to help solve this problem," Mayor Travis McDermott said. "But we have realistic hurdles that we would have to overcome, and even with our best intentions, we can't escape it."
One big question, he said, is where would a Pallet Village be located.
"People are not going to want you to use the land behind their house to build this," McDermott said. "That's just a simple fact."
Councilman Jay Bancroft expressed similar thoughts.
"I hope we'll be very sensitive to local opposition that is likely to be an issue," Bancroft said. "I think this idea of making it look suitable to the neighbors is important for this education campaign, for us to take steps that we've been talking about for a long time"
Councilman Jason Lawhorn noted that the Georgetown Pallet Village was built near where there was already a large established homeless encampment. He said it's important to understand the scale of homelessness in Newark to better understand whether a Pallet Village would be utilized here.
He added that city staffers are already overworked and questioned whether the city should have a role in creating a Pallet Village.
"I love the program," he said. "I have reservations about how we execute it in Newark."
Suchanec asked his colleagues to direct City Manager Tom Coleman to prepare a report on whether there are any city-owned properties that could potentially be used for a Pallet Village. He suggested looking at underutilized parks as well as a piece of land the city recently purchased off Paper Mill Road, between the city's electric substation and White Clay Creek.
Ultimately, the council decided that in order to not burden city employees, each council member will compile of list of possible locations in their district for further study.
"You can find so many reasons to say no for something," Suchanec said. "The easy thing is to say no or to convince yourself this is something not worth doing. All I'm saying is take a baby step. Find out if we have any locations in this city where something like this could happen."

Water park renovation cost, timeline, vex council

 Another summer of water park dormancy in Chesapeake Beach could stretch into year three if the price isn't right.On June 12 the mayor and town council received a second presentation from a consultant about how to improve the 30-year-old facility, which was closed in 2023 by the previous administration.
"We know it needs to be done, we are trying to find the most efficient way to do it," Mark Wilkerson of Paddock Pool Company told the town council during the presentation.
In April the council allocated $60,000 for the consultant to explore the feasibility of bringing the facility back to life.
Wilkerson said a design team was hired and geo-technology engineers examined the pilings on which the park is located.
"The intent is to use the existing piling system," Wilkerson said.
The consultant provided town officials with two concepts.
Wilkerson said the Concept A is "basically, the park as it is now, with some changes that came from the waterpark committee, from public works, other interested parties and my team as well."
The changes would include a new slide and what Wilkerson described as improved park circulation.
Wilkerson described many of the components of Concept B as being friendlier to the area's aging population, with more shade, underwater benches, increased deck space and speed control for the park's "lazy river."
Wilkerson said of potential changes to the facility, "It will never be perfect because I can't make the ground any bigger." He said the town will "make the best use of the space we have."
The uncertain price tag of the renovation project prompted one council member to speak up.
"I think it would be irresponsible for this council to continue with additional funding without knowing what this project costs," Councilman Eric Reinhardt said. "We need to know what it's going to cost up front before we're dumping additional money into it. The water park has never been a profitable enterprise."
Reinhardt added that while he understood the water park is part of Chesapeake Beach's "DNA, the best path is not going as fast as we can."
Councilman Jamey Shuls said the town does need to do something.
"We know the water park is not repairable," Shuls said, adding that to do nothing would leave a park "rotting in front of our eyes."
Councilwoman Laura Blackwelder said she would prefer the recommended demolition be part of the contract for any renovation project, rather than possibly working with two separate contractors.
Wilkerson said he would return to the council for their July meeting and provide cost estimates.

title: Legacy Bricks Honor Military Veterans, Memorialize the Fallen
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Legacy Bricks honor military veterans, memorialize the fallen

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News

 Memorial Day remembers U.S. servicemen and servicewomen who lost their lives defending this country's freedom and, as is the tradition, they will be honored during ceremonies at American Legions, VFWs, churches and so forth.At the North East Community Park, however, fallen servicemen and servicewomen are memorialized every day of the year — not just on Memorial Day. A spotlight also shines there on U.S. military veterans in general. That's because there is a flag-court-style monument comprised of bricks bearing the engraved names of those who made the supreme sacrifice, as well as of those who are veterans.
Dedicated last July 3 during the town's Salute to Cecil County Veterans ceremony and fireworks show, the monument at the base of a tall pole holding the U.S. flag and the MIA-POW banner is known as the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial.
"North East town leaders understand the importance of memorializing those who paid the ultimate price and of honoring those who served. Many of those bricks out there are in memory of those who lost their lives defending the United States. Other bricks honor those who served in the military. Every person who ever served in the military took an oath — I will risk my life defending this country," emphasized Gene Daley, who is commander of the North East Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) Post 6027.
Daley, who served in the U.S. Army from 1986 through 1995, when he received his honorable discharge at the rank of staff sergeant, noted that North East VFW contributed one of the engraved bricks that make up the memorial.
"We have a brick out there for POWs-MIAs. They never returned from war and it's likely that most, if not all, are dead," said Daley, who is a 1985 North East High School graduate.
Of the more than 500 bricks cobbled together to create that special 320-square-foot area in the park, about 200 bricks already have been inscribed with names and other information about those servicemen and servicewomen who died while defending this country or about the military veterans. Each brick was bought for $75 by relatives of veterans and of those who lost their lives in service. They were purchased between November 2023 and January 2024 — the first ordering period.
About 40 engraved bricks were added recently, reflecting purchases made by families between November 2024 and January 2025, marking the second wave. Every year, during a two-month period that starts on Veterans Day in November and ends on New Year's Day in January, relatives of servicemen and servicewoman who paid the ultimate price or of military veterans can purchase legacy bricks to honor their loved ones.
There are approximately 250 blank bricks right now, and they serve as placeholders for future Legacy Brick purchases. Once ordered, the company engraves the requested message on a brick and ships it to North East. Then a blank, placeholder brick is removed from the monument and the inscribed brick is put in its place.
"This installation provides a lasting tribute to the men and women who have contributed to our nation's freedom. It covers every single major military conflict, dating back to World War I. Anytime we, as a town, can honor a legacy, it's a powerful thing," said North East Assistant Town Administrator Grant Handley.
North East Mayor Kelly Benson commented, "These Legacy Bricks honor those in our community who have made the most selfless sacrifice of servicing our country. It is a privilege to have this memorial in our community park."
Some of the inscribed bricks honor or memorialize servicemen and servicewoman who are or were Cecil County natives. Common information engraved on the bricks include name, branch of military, rank and duration of service and, when applicable, the conflict in which he or she served or in which he or she perished while serving.
"There also are personal messages on the Legacy Bricks, like, 'We miss you'," Handley said. "Some include cool nicknames, like 'Hell on Wheels', and the nicknames typically have something to do with the units that they served with."
The idea for a central monument in the park came about after Gold Star families had submitted plaques honoring their loved ones and asked the town to display them. Steve Riley, who works for Entech Engineering and is the town's contracted engineer, designed the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial.
"He did it for free, which was awesome. It was his way of contributing," Handley said.
The construction of the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial was included in a series of North East Community Park upgrades that totaled $343,828 and was covered by a combination of grants and other sources, such as the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). The overall project included two sand volleyball courts, a horseshoe pit, renovation of public bathrooms, new playground equipment, exercise stations along the walking trail, new handicap-accessible sidewalks and ramps to easily access park pavilions.
Daley is thankful that he served in the Army, explaining, "It gave me the confidence to do things that I didn't think I could ever do. It gave discipline. The military gives you a way to conduct yourself in your life."
One of the bricks in that town park memorial bears the name of Daley's late father, Felix Daley, who served in the U.S. Navy for about 20 years, starting during World War II. That brick, reflecting Felix Daley's service to his country, is a point of pride for his son and for his other surviving relatives.
As for Memorial Day, Daley commented, "It is important that we remember those who gave their lives for our country. The surviving parents, husbands, wives, brothers, sisters and children will always feel that loss. Memorial Day is akin to the day when someone important to you dies. We must always remember them."
For more information on how to order a Legacy Brick, call 410-287-5801, ext 7106.

title: Cambridge Indivisible Aims to Teach Members About Civics, Cofounder Says
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge Indivisible aims to teach members about civics, cofounder says

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CAMBRIDGE — For Cambridge Indivisible cofounder and Cochair Michelle Fowle, it's about understanding the power you have."I think the really important thing is for people to understand the power that they actually hold," she said. "So that's kind of my focus. And I'm doing that here."
When Fowle moved to Cambridge from California with her husband, Andy, in September, the two hit the ground running to form Cambridge Indivisible, which is a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Fowle said the overarching goal of the group is to give people a place to build community and learn about civics. She said everyone is welcome.
"We have Republicans who are showing up now at our protests, asking how they can help," she said. "And I embrace them."
Mentioning health care and housing, Fowle said there are issues that people on both sides of the aisle can unite on. She said that for her, the organization isn't about identity politics.
"We don't have to agree," she said. "In fact, we shouldn't agree. And it's healthy to have that conversation. I'm not trying to make you be me."
There was a time when Fowle knew very little about politics.
"They say that there's two days that are critical in your life," she said. "It's the day you're born and the day you find out why. And in November 2016, I found out why."
Fowle said the 2016 general election results thrust her into a world of activism after not paying close attention to politics for many years. While living in California, Fowle learned from other organizers, helped put on rallies and marches, and built relationships with elected officials.
"For somebody who didn't know anything, I can teach it now," she said.
MAKING WAVES
In recent months, Cambridge Indivisible has garnered attention over events it has hosted around town. During one event in March, the chapter hosted Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) for a town hall.
The chapter also has hosted multiple rallies to criticize elected federal leadership. That criticism has been largely directed toward Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) for not holding in-person town halls for his constituents. Harris hosted multiple virtual town halls in the past two months.
Fowle said the Cambridge chapter of Indivisible has more than 1,000 members from across the Eastern Shore. She said there is no formal registration process to be a member.
Cambridge Indivisible Treasurer Ilia Johnson said she joined the chapter this year to get more representation for the Hispanic community in the area and to support her neighbors. She said she likes that Cambridge Indivisible is a group "for everybody."
"All we want to do is what's best for everybody," she said.
During a Cambridge Indivisible rally held along U.S. Route 50 in Cambridge on April 19, Gloria McVeigh said she joined the chapter after Harris was elected in November. She said it's a nice group that holds the same values as herself.
Although there have been disapproving shouts from people driving their cars past Cambridge Indivisible rallies these past few months, Fowle said the chapter hasn't faced much opposition other than from Harris.
In the past, Harris has shared his criticisms of and concerns with the Indivisible organization as a whole.
Following a Cambridge Indivisible rally held March 13 that called on Harris to hold an in-person town hall and questioned his allegiance to his constituents, Harris alleged those at the rally were "brought in by buses" and not his constituents. He said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's goingon" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there.
"This is AstroTurf," Harris said about the organization in March. "This is not grassroots."
Fowle said the chapter does get internet trolls on its public page, and she deletes their comments and blocks them.
"It's like listen, when this hits you — and it will — I'll be there for you if you want," she said about the internet trolls.

title: Piscataway Conoy Tribe Receives Land Donation
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Piscataway Conoy Tribe receives land donation

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 581
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After a long process, it's official — a property on Country Lane in Waldorf will be donated to the Piscataway Conoy Tribe.The donation did not come easily, as tensions rose between a split tribe, with a number coming out to oppose it.
Charles County first received notification about the land donation request in January 2020 and sent correspondence about the process on Feb. 5, 2020.
On July 29, 2020, the county sent the first of four lease renewal documents between then and March 16, 2022. Despite several attempts at communication between the county and the tribe, the two sides were unable to come to a formal agreement.
A letter said the plot of land had been a center for indigenous culture with biannual pow-wows from 1982 through 2014, as well as school field trips and other public events.
The letter also stated that the Cedarville Band was required to jump through "numerous bureaucratic hoops," including paying $10,000 for a land survey.
The American Civil Liberties Union requested the county stop a planned eviction and work toward a long-term solution to donate the land to the Cedarville Band of Piscataway Indians.
"Returning the land would affirmatively recognize and show appreciation for the people who have been preserving American history and Indigenous American culture on this land," the ACLU letter stated.
The site is divided with approximately 9.5 acres in Charles County and 7 acres in Prince George's County.
"The property being proposed for transfer is located in both Prince George's and Charles counties. The property is owned entirely by Charles County, and so there is no approval needed from Prince George's County in order to complete the transfer," Danielle Mitchell, an attorney with Charles County government, told Southern Maryland News earlier this year.
During a public hearing last month, a large number of the Piscataway were split on what to do with the land.
From the 1950s through the 1970s, the property was owned by the U.S. Army and used as a Nike Battery site.
Rosanna Swann, the first speaker of the hearing, said at the time she opposed the land donation because of a court case between Jesse James Swann Jr. and Francis Gray, who both lead different portions of the Piscataway people.
Rosanna Swann also pointed to the site as a potential "environmental disaster" due to its military history and said that the area was contaminated and could cost anywhere from $4 to $10 million to clean up.
Gray, the chairman of the Piscataway Conoy Tribe, said, "We the Piscataway Conoy people welcome this opportunity as it will finally provide a much needed home base. … It runs deeper than that. It will provide a means for the preservation of our identity."
Later in the night, Acting County Administrator Deborah Hall said that the federal government covers the cleanup of the contaminated land.
Many others came up and supported the donation, citing the importance of giving the Piscataway people a land base so other tribes can find them.
County attorneys reported that there were well over 200 written comments on the matter, and that sentiments were very split on if the land should be donated.
On May 6, it was time to put it to a vote.
Commissioner Gilbert "BJ" Bowling (D) told tribe members in attendance that he would be abstaining from the vote.
"I don't feel it's appropriate for me to get in the middle of it," Bowling said, citing disagreement between sects of the tribe and the ongoing legal dispute.
The other four commissioners voted yes, passing the resolution and giving the tribe a land base.

 CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.

title: Maryland Session Concludes with Balanced Budget
author: Marissa Yelenik and Sofia Appolonio Capital News Service
content:
Maryland session concludes with balanced budget

 Author/Byline: Marissa Yelenik and Sofia Appolonio Capital News Service | Section: State News
