 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers passed a budget on Monday, concluding their spring session after months of grappling with a tough fiscal reality and new federal policies.The end-of-session agreement hikes taxes and cuts programs to balance the spending plan for the 2026 fiscal year, assuming the federal funding picture does not change radically in the months to come.
Lawmakers made the budget work partly by trimming back the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the ambitious 2021 education reform plan meant to improve public schools. Architects of the deal said the changes will preserve the Blueprint's priorities.
"We present a budget that puts Maryland in a strong fiscal position and faces the challenges ahead while protecting our shared values and priorities," said Senate Budget and Taxation Chair Guy Guzzone. (D-Howard).
But House Minority Whip Del. Jesse Pippy (R-Frederick, Carroll) argued that the plan unnecessarily burdens taxpayers.
"A majority of my colleagues feel very strongly that we could have balanced the budget without raising taxes," Pippy said. "I don't think the direction of the state is the direction that most Marylanders want to go in."
Republicans made their mark on legislative work in the opening months of the new presidential administration, which helped give rise to the newly formed Maryland Freedom Caucus.
Still, the Democrat-controlled legislature generally opposed President Donald Trump's policies.
The state — home to the most federal workers in the country outside of Washington, D.C. — likely faces continuing challenges with the Trump administration's mass government layoffs. At present, one Democratic leader said, the number of fired workers in Maryland stands at about 11,000.
"We expect that number to climb to 30,000, and there are many more contractors, probably at least double that amount," said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard, Montgomery).
The legislature might have to reconvene at some point this year to cope with unemployment and changes in federal policy affecting Maryland. For now, though, the General Assembly has settled a range of issues.
BUDGET
The $67 billion spending plan addresses a significant deficit through approximately $2 billion in spending cuts and $1.6 billion in tax changes.
The budget raises income taxes on the state's higher earners, extends the sales tax to certain technology services and introduces a $5 tire fee. It includes two new tax brackets, increases the standard deduction, phases out itemized deductions for those in higher tax brackets and includes tax hikes on individual goods and services.
Many lawmakers celebrated its passage, but some said increasing the standard deduction would lead to service cuts in lower-income counties that rely on the income tax of low- and middle-income residents. The finalized plan will now go to Moore for consideration.
ENERGY
Energy was a hot topic this session as lawmakers worked to address high energy prices. They passed a three-bill package on Monday.
The package focuses on new in-state energy generation, ratepayer protections and reforms, solar siting and permitting and the creation of a state energy planning office. It outlines procurement processes for nuclear, battery storage and dispatchable energy, and removes trash incineration from the state's Renewable Portfolio Standard.
"I think, on balance, it's a good package," said Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Senate Education, Energy and the Environment committee.
The package initially drew criticism from environmental advocates, who were concerned one of the bills would lead to new natural gas development in the state. But the Chesapeake Climate Action Network Action Fund praised the bill as passed, saying in a statement that it "will likely reduce the chance of new gas plant construction in the state and … will advance a host of clean energy priorities," including battery storage.
Republican critics worry that the package doesn't do enough to help ratepayers.
EDUCATION
Blueprint funding was the subject of debate during the legislative session. In January, Moore proposed short-term cuts to mitigate the cost of the massive education plan, pushing back and pausing funding for different programs.
The education budget came under even more scrutiny late in the session when an expected $418 million in federal funds was suddenly in jeopardy. U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon announced the end of a pandemic-era fund for state educational spending.
As it stands, state lawmakers agreed to postpone the Blueprint requirement that teachers receive a set amount of planning every school week, delaying it for three years. Additional Blueprint funding was decreased through freezes and cuts.
JUSTICE SYSTEM
Lawmakers passed a bill to let prisoners access medical or geriatric parole more easily by allowing them to prove they are no longer a threat to others. It would not apply to those serving life sentences without parole or those on the sex offender registry. Geriatric parole would only be available to those over 65 who have served at least 20 years of their sentence.
Lawmakers also approved the Maryland Second Look Act, which aimed to reduce the sentences of some inmates with good behavior credits.
A proposal to scale back the state's practice of automatically sentencing teen offenders as adults in violent crimes stalled in committee. The bill faced pushback from law enforcement over concerns that the Department of Juvenile Services couldn't accommodate juveniles with "complex problems."
PRIVACY
Concerns over the Trump administration's immigration policy encouraged some lawmakers to propose the Maryland Data Privacy Act to prevent law enforcement and other local officials from sharing sensitive data with immigration officers. The bill failed to receive enough support.
Despite concerns about unregulated police drones, lawmakers decided not to advance a proposal to set guidelines for law enforcement uses of aerial surveillance.
DISABILITIES
Lawmakers passed Eric's ID Law — a measure allowing individuals with invisible disabilities to include a sticker on the bottom of their license, identification or moped operator's permit. The notation is meant to improve interactions and communication with law enforcement.
REPARATIONS
Maryland lawmakers approved the creation of a commission to study the impact of slavery after years of debate and consideration. The Maryland Reparations Commission would make recommendations to the state legislature, providing guidance on what, if any, benefits should be given to those impacted by historical inequality by November 2027.
SEX ABUSE
After emotional deliberation, lawmakers voted to downsize the monetary compensation the state can provide for sexual abuse lawsuits, amending the amount survivors can file for under the 2023 Child Victims Act.
GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE
Republicans introduced a bill that would have made it a felony for a healthcare provider to give hormone replacement therapy to any minor, but the measure did not pass.
If passed, the Fairness in Girls' Sports Act would have required both public schools and the nonpublic schools that compete against them to separate sports teams based on the team members' sex assigned at birth. Similar legislation has been introduced since 2022.
The General Assembly turned away a bill to allow "X" as a sex designation on birth certificates for transgender and nonbinary individuals.

Maryland officials worry about 'chaos' to come

 ANNAPOLIS — The Maryland General Assembly just concluded its scheduled spring session, but Democratic leaders are already looking ahead to an uncertain future driven by President Donald Trump's "chaos."In comments to reporters, Gov. Wes Moore boasted about the legislature's accomplishments — stressing that Trump's shadow still looms.
"You cannot talk about those things without acknowledging the chaos that is taking place in Washington, D.C.," Moore told reporters.
Maryland could potentially lose the new FBI building it was supposed to get, while also facing stock market volatility and a tariff policy Moore described as a "national sales tax."
"While I'm thankful for the progress we've made in this session, we know that protecting Marylanders, and caring for Marylanders and defending Marylanders does not happen over 90 days," Moore said.
Lawmakers in the waning hours of the session announced the formation of a Joint Federal Action Oversight Committee, a bipartisan group will be tasked with monitoring the ripple effects of the federal government on Maryland.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) told reporters lawmakers have spent this session bracing for external threats.
"We have been working this year to protect the state of Maryland against the draconian slash and burn actions of the Trump administration," Ferguson said. "And with Elon Musk, who has been talking about efficiency, but really destroying Marylanders' lives."
Fear of Trump and Musk's plans also loomed large in the minds of Democrats on the Senate floor, as debate heated up in advance of Monday's midnight deadline for adjournment.
In a conversation about how to help laid-off federal workers, Sen. Jim Rosapepe argued that it's hard to work out cost estimates in the current political climate.
"It's hard to estimate this because we don't know how much damage Mr. Musk and his merry band are going to do," said Rosapepe (D-Prince George's, Anne Arundel).
Senate Republican Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) interrupted to say, "I know, you've said that a few times."
Rosapepe raised his voice.
"That's the important point here," he said. "It's unclear what these people in Washington are doing to our state."
"We know it's bad," he said, "but we don't know how bad it's going to be."

 After rallies in the last month called on Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) to hold an in-person town hall, Harris opened a channel of communication with constituents Tuesday evening to answer questions and hear concerns.The telephone town hall was attended by more than 10,000 people, Harris said. He said the reason he likes doing telephone town halls rather than in-person town halls is because more people are able to attend without having to leave their homes.
"Far many more (people) than we could ever do in any other venue," Harris said.
During the hour-long telephone town hall, Harris heard from around 15 people. Those who called in only gave their first names, with some sharing where they live.
Many concerns and questions raised during the town hall dealt with recent federal layoffs, the fate of programs like Social Security and Medicaid, recent actions taken by the Trump administration and Harris' voting history. Some of the people who spoke shared their criticisms of Harris.
One caller, identified as James, shared concerns about the recent announcements of funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health. He said "fundamental" NIH discoveries fuel the pharmaceutical industry and without the funds to make those discoveries, the pharmaceutical industry will "collapse."
"Trump has sent his idiots from the Department of Governmental Elimination into our fundamental medical research," James said, referencing the Department of Government Efficiency. "And this will destroy the fundamental formation of discovering drugs in this country. So, Congressman Harris, wake up."
After sharing he thinks Elon Musk — who heads the Department of Government Efficiency — shouldn't be called an idiot, Harris said the Trump administration wants to reduce overhead costs, which he believes would allow the federal government to spend more money on research.
Harris, a former physician who was an NIH-funded researcher, said institutions who receive a research grant can get as much as 80% in additional funding for overhead. He said there should be a cap on that overhead funding.
"To me, that's taking advantage of the federal government," he said. "And if we can cap the overhead, it allows us to actually spend more money on actual research projects, not on administrative costs."
Another caller, identified as Allison from Wicomico County, asked what Harris is doing to protect his constituents' data that may have been accessed by the Department of Government Efficiency.
Allison brought up the recent rally Cambridge Indivisible held in Cambridge to demand he hold a town hall. She said Harris "blatantly lied" that the protesters at the rally were bused in and not his constituents.
As she continued to talk about how she knew many of the people at the rally, Harris tried to speak. As Allison continued speaking, Harris said he was sorry, but he would have to mute her.
"Look, if you're going to filibuster, I have to cut you off," he said before muting her.
Harris then said there was a bus, funded by Indivisible, going to Cambridge, adding "there's no question in anyone's mind" about that.
Cambridge Indivisible Co-Founder and Co-Chair Michelle Fowle has said many of those at the rally were her neighbors who live in Cambridge.
In response to Allison's question about personal data, Harris said there are multiple government organizations, like the IRS, that have access to citizens' personal data. He said the Department of Government Efficiency has accessed people's birth dates to identify "fraud, waste and abuse."
"I would hope that everybody wants waste, fraud and abuse uncovered," he said.
Harris instructed those that he wasn't able to hear from during the event to stay on the line after so their question could be recorded and his office could get back to them.

 CAMBRIDGE — Energy was high as Eastern Shore residents packed the gymnasium at Mace's Lane Middle School Saturday for Cambridge Indivisible and Eastern Shore Indivisible's town hall event with Maryland U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.)."I know I was not your first choice," Raskin said over cheers from the crowd. "I heard your congressman couldn't quite squeeze you in today."
Raskin represents most of Montgomery County and part of Prince George's County. Cambridge Indivisible Co-Founder and Co-Chair Michelle Fowle said the organization invited Maryland U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) — who represents the Eastern Shore and lives in Cambridge — but Harris didn't respond.
"We made it super easy for him to be here, and he didn't even have the decency to formally decline," Fowle said. "He just completely ignores us and just tells everybody that we're paid $40 an hour and bused in."
Although Harris wasn't at the Cambridge Indivisible event Saturday, he is holding a telephone hall for residents on Tuesday, March 25. Those who would like to attend the event, which will be from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., can listen in by calling 833-380-0671 or can stream the event at harris.house.gov/live.
During the town hall Saturday, Raskin expressed concerns with the Republican Party's priorities.
He brought up recent actions taken by President Donald Trump and the Department of Government Efficiency. He said he is trying to "stop this savage assault on American democracy."
"They're not opponents of corruption," Raskin said. "They're agents of corruption."
When it came to the question and answer portion of the town hall, residents asked what could be done in response to the Trump administration's actions.
Many made a point to mention they were not paid to be there, referencing Harris' words following a rally Cambridge Indivisible organized in opposition to the congressman March 13. Harris told members of the media he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents, adding that he believed they were paid protesters "brought in by buses."
Commenting on the Saturday town hall, Harris said in a statement Monday that it's "ironic" that "ultra-radical leftist" Raskin is "suddenly pretending to care about our farmers, watermen and people on the Eastern Shore after four years of voting for reckless Biden administration policies and radical environmental regulations — which almost crushed our Eastern Shore economy."
"If these protests weren't being paid for and influenced by radical Democrat activists, Jaime Raskin would have stayed on the western shore — right where he and his radical policies belong," Harris said.
Throughout the event Saturday, volunteers were available with smart phones to capture residents' stories.
"Andy Harris can ignore our emails, he can dodge our phone calls and he can refuse to hold a town hall," Cambridge Indivisible Co-Founder and Co-Chair Andy Fowle said. "But he cannot erase our stories."
Retired East New Market resident Roscoe Handy, who attended the event, said he has concerns about the fate of Social Security, Medicare and the U.S. Department of Education. He said Harris needs to hear from his constituents and put a face to their name.
"I didn't necessarily vote for him. However, I'm in his district," said Handy, a Democrat.
At the end of the event, Raskin was asked if he has plans to run for president in the next U.S. presidential election.
"I will do whatever is necessary for us to save our democracy," he said in response as applause and cheers filled the room.

title: Angela Alsobrooks Talks With Eastern Shore Municipalities About Concerns
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Angela Alsobrooks talks with Eastern Shore Municipalities about concerns

 EASTON — U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D) met with multiple municipal leaders from across the Eastern Shore to discuss issues they face.In addition to meeting with multiple municipalities, Alsobrooks visited Eastern Shore agricultural leaders and participated in a tour of Chesapeake College. She met with higher education leaders during her stop at the college.
Alsobrooks heard concerns of municipal officials including the freezing and cutting of Federal Emergency Management Agency funds and how U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on the Eastern Shore can affect the agricultural economy and area families.
"It's so important today to be here and to have conversations," Alsobrooks said. "We spent the day here very intentionally to hear from farmers, to hear from business owners, to hear from municipal leaders, who are primarily sharing the impact of some of the federal cuts that we've seen and that we've seen in some of the freezing of funds."
Multiple municipalities voiced their concerns about the freezing and cuts of federal funding. One big project on the Eastern Shore is the Ocean City beach replenishment project.
According to Ocean City officials, the beach replenishment project was first started in 1989 and is a partnership between the federal government, the state of Maryland, Worcester County and Ocean City.
The project was built to protect the shoreline along the Ocean City coastline. It consists of building a dune system, a seawall and pumping sand on the beach to provide protection from storms.
The project has estimated to save $1 billion in property damage since its completion in 1991. Every year in the winter, Ocean City conducts the project, but the federal funding for this winter project has not been received.
Another concern brought to Alsobrooks was the funding freeze for the Shore Resiliency program by FEMA.
According to Cambridge officials, the plan for the project includes three main elements: a living shoreline, earth and rock embankments and stormwater management to alleviate flooding.
Almost 30% of the design for the Cambridge program is done, but the funds for that project has been frozen.
Another concern brought to Alsobrooks was helping kids who experience immigrant enforcement with their parents and how immigrant enforcement will effect the economy on the Eastern Shore.
Salisbury officials mentioned two men on work visas with families who were picked up by ICE and that have already been shipped to New Orleans. The officials are concerned about how the agricultural economy can be affected.
Another story mentioned was about two daughters a 5- and 7-year-old whose parents were picked up by ICE. The children lived at home for two days without mentioning anything to school officials.
Alsobrooks listened to all concerns and what what she plans to do and how important their concerns are to the state.
"I'm going to be working to make sure that I really do what I can to to get those funds unfrozen and to continue to stay in communication with leaders and community of members to help our state be successful," she said.
Officials voiced appreciation for Alsobrooks listening and her promise to continue to communicate with leaders on the Eastern Shore.
"It's really important that the senator hears from small communities here in the Eastern Shore," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook. "It feels like she's really taking our concerns seriously into heart, and she's going to find the answers to our questions."

title: Museum Effort 'On Pause' After Project Lead Fined for Falsely Claiming to Be an Architect
author: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com
content:
Museum effort 'on pause' after project lead fined for falsely claiming to be an architect

 March 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 970
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON — The Elkton Colored School Museum project has been put on hold after the Maryland Board of Architects issued a $20,000 fine against Dale Glenwood Green, the project's architect, for falsely representing himself as a licensed architect for at least 17 years. The board said that his claims have led to Green stealing opportunities from qualified architects, such as the museum project.The ECS Museum project had been working in partnership with an architecture firm that Green was a part of, during which partnership Green gave a tour of the ECS building to Gov. Moore during his visit last year to Cecil County. Due to the fine against Green and his lack of licensing, the project has been put on hold.
"We are on pause right now because we can't move forward until we find out what is going to be done architecturally for the benefit of the group and the benefit of putting the building in place where it's supposed to be," said Town of Elkton Commissioner Charles Givens, an ECS alumni who has been heavily involved in the museum project. "We're dependent upon grants and other finances to move forward…we aren't going to get funds until the mess that we have right now is cleared up."
Green is known for working to preserve the oldest Black communities in Maryland, and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore appointed him to the board of directors for the Maryland African American Museum Corporation.
Green also claimed to have a Ph.D in architecture and historic preservation from the University of Missouri, but the school has no record of his enrollment according to an article by the Baltimore Banner.
Until being fired recently, Green had taught architecture and historic preservation at Morgan State University since 2008, where he earned his undergraduate degree in architecture. Baltimore architect Jerryn McCray was teaching as an adjunct professor at Morgan State when he met Green as an undergraduate nearly 20 years ago.
"He was the best salesman I think I've ever met, but his work was just awful," McCray said.
McCray acted as a mentor for Green in one class, but said "his ego would never allow him to see himself as a mentee. He took the position as if he was already a professional. He dressed the part, wore a bow tie, the suit, the whole get up that he still carries."
Shortly after graduating from Morgan State, Green started a company and listed himself as the principal project architect on the website. McCray recalled confronting him for marketing himself as an architect, and proceeded to file a complaint with the state against Green in 2008 when the website went unchanged.
However, the state did not have a record of the initial complaint and nothing came of it, till now.
McCray said that Green has continued to cause problems for himself and other architects in the community since then.
"He's persisted to find different ways to promote himself as an architect," McCray said. "It had gotten to the point where it was affecting my company, the local economy, my family, my relationships…I had to make it stop."
According to McCray, because of the way Green presented himself and played the part, he became connected with a lot of people in the industry, which took away opportunities from legitimately licensed architects like McCray.
"It's been more of an obstacle dealing with Dale, in terms of my business, than it's been being Black and being an architect," McCray said.
McCray recalled telling several architects who partnered with Green that he is not licensed or trustworthy.
"They look at me like I'm the issue, and it's ruined those relationships for 20 years, and I've persisted to speak the truth. I know that Dale is a con artist," McCray said.
McCray filed a second complaint when a national architectural firm was reviewing Green's application for a renovation project and upon reviewing his credentials, found mismatched fonts and a license that seemed fraudulent. The project manager reached out to McCray, who proceeded to look up Green's license number, which was associated with a woman living in Georgia. After speaking with her, both filed complaints which led to a state investigation on Green.
The investigation into Green began in the spring of 2023, culminating in a final order issued by the board in December of 2024. The board increased the fine from $15,000 to $20,000, insisting on the maximum penalty for each violation because of Green's "incessant bad faith" which persisted for at least 17 years.
The Maryland Board of Architects determined that Green did in fact forge a license to practice architecture, and even created a fake email chain blaming one of his former students for the fraudulent license.
The fine is the largest issued by the Maryland Board of Architects since 2012.
A main focus of the case was on the testimony of Stanford Britt, the president of Sulton Campbell Britt & Associates, that he had hired Green to manage the firm's website and help with technological aspects of the company, a firm at which Green had been claiming to be a vice president and partner.
Britt testified that he never promoted Green to a partner of the firm. Currently, the firm website lists Green as vice president and partner, with Britt the only other listed employee. Britt said that his architecture license had expired three years prior to the trial and he was now working as a teacher in Virginia.
According to Givens, Green reached out to the Elkton Colored School Museum team to set up a meeting and discuss next steps in the upcoming weeks.
"It's thrown a wrench in the plan because he was one of the architects for the company and right now we are at a stand still," Givens said.
Givens compared the situation to buying a Mercedes that breaks down on your way home, unexpected and disappointing.
Green and his firm did not respond to a request for comment.

 In the struggle between historic sidewalks in Port Deposit and the Americans with Disabilities Act, the ADA wins, according to the Maryland State Highway Administration.SHA has two projects in progress in Port Deposit; one to remediate flooding and the second to make stretches of sidewalk handicapped accessible. This will mean either leveling heaving granite stones or removing them entirely.
Vicky Rinkerman, town administrator, said that in this early phase SHA engineers have reported that the town's existing historic granite sidewalks and curbing are central to the study.

Questions to be answered by the SHA include whether or not there would there be a flap gate to prevent back flow, and if the catch basin and the drain pipe need to be enlarged.

 Considering no one present knew the departed, the modest turnout last week for a burial in a Lusby cemetery was remarkable.The Feb. 27 service at Middleham and St. Peter's Cemetery was drawn from the Book of Common Prayer, which was used often during the last quarter of the 19th century. That may have been the time when remains interred was part of a live person.
"I believe it was from somebody's private cemetery when the cliffs used to be way, way out," George Oliver told Southern Maryland News.
Oliver, who resides in Chesapeake Ranch Estates, frequently visits beach areas at the base of the cliffs, mostly in search of sharks' teeth and other fossils.
The Alabama native recalled the discovery of what turned out to be a coffin containing human remains at the edge of the Chesapeake Bay.
"I found it in November and discovered there was a skeleton in it," Oliver said. "I had been seeing it for months. It was sitting up out of the water. I just thought it was wood filled with sand."
Oliver said he contacted local law enforcement and was told of his find, "You can have it. There's nothing there."
Notifications were made to Calvert Marine Museum and the Calvert County Historical Society.
"Our parish was contacted several weeks ago by the county historic planner, Christopher Sperling," Hugh Davies, a parishioner at Middleham and St. Peter's, said. "He informed us that the county had received the remains of an unknown person and asked if they might be reinterred in the Middleham cemetery. The church had provided such a reinterment over 10 years ago."
Oliver also had been involved with that discovery.
"In 2008, we found a leg," Oliver said, adding that he had hoped the leg was missing from the remains he had found in late last year. However, remains of two legs were identified from that find.
Other information provided by the church stated the best estimate of the time of the coffin and remains is the late 19th century.
Church officials reported that a general conclusion reached is that the person "was likely a Christian" and that reinterment was needed. The Lusby church was deemed the most appropriate place for the interment, in part since Middleham Chapel is the oldest church building in Calvert County, dating back to 1684.
Pastor Erin Betz Shank, priest in charge at the parish, recited the service drawn from the Book of Common Prayer.
A white cloth bag containing the bones located within the coffin was re-placed in the coffin and attendees were invited to deposit handfuls of earth into the grave.
"We therefore commit their body to the ground, earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust," Shank recited during the service, which included the reciting of the Lord's Prayer.

title: Maryland Considers Shake-Up in How Judges Are Picked
author: Paul Kiefer Capital News Service
content:
Maryland considers shake-up in how judges are picked

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1253
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers are weighing two bills this year that would shake up how the state chooses circuit court judges.The proposals are at odds with one another. One bill aims to adjust the existing contested election process for circuit court judges by opening primaries to all Maryland voters. The other would eliminate contested circuit court elections altogether — a shift that would require a constitutional amendment.
The proposals represent two sides of a decades-long debate in the Maryland General Assembly about the value of contested circuit court elections.
Some members of Maryland's judiciary argue doing away with judicial elections entirely would shield judges from the ethical and practical challenges involved in competitive political campaigns.
"The job of a judge is, or at least should be, inherently apolitical," said Maryland Supreme Court Chief Justice Matthew J. Fader.
Others stand by Maryland's approach to filling circuit court benches, arguing that contested elections are a valuable opportunity for voters to shape their judiciary.
Circuit court judges are currently the only Maryland court to run in contested elections. All other state courts fill their benches with judges appointed by the governor, giving voters a say in whether those judges hold their seats in retention elections every 10 years. But the judges run unopposed and, at least according to some of the state's leading legal experts, no Maryland judge has been ousted in a retention election in living memory.
While the governor appoints judges to fill vacancies on circuit courts, the state constitution requires those judges stand for reelection every 15 years — elections in which they, unlike any other Maryland judge, can face a challenger.
The conversation about the system's merits has restarted among Maryland lawmakers, with Fader and other prominent Maryland legal figures backing a bill that would change circuit courts' process for filling benches to match the rest of Maryland courts.
The proposal arose from a work group formed by the Maryland Judicial Conference three years ago to review the issue. The work group released its final report — which argued that Maryland should move away from contested circuit court elections — last year.
"We believe that this is the best solution to maintain public trust and confidence in the court and in its ability to have judges who are fully qualified to take office in all cases," Fader told members of the House Judiciary Committee in a preliminary hearing on the bill.
Proponents of the bill assert that contested elections for circuit court positions open the bench to candidates who are unqualified for the role.
"Our system allows individuals with little to no judicial experience to challenge sitting judges," said Prince George's County Circuit Court Judge Cheri Simpkins. That means some judges who were initially appointed to their seat "must run against opponents who only meet the minimum qualifications of being a licensed person residing in the county for five years and paying a nominal filing fee," she added.
Maryland State Bar Association President Raphael Santini pointed to former Prince George's County Circuit Court Judge April Ademiluyi, who won her seat in a contested election in 2020 and whose "egregious" violations of judicial ethics prompted the Maryland Supreme Court to remove her from the bench in 2024.
Appointed judges, Santini told Capital News Service, have passed through a rigorous vetting process run by a judicial nominating commission and more than a dozen committees within the state's bar association. That vetting is done by fellow attorneys from a variety of legal fields who are well-equipped to review a candidate's legal and personal record, he added.
Elizabeth Hewlett, an attorney in Prince George's County and supporter of the proposal, said that voter participation in circuit court races is vastly lower than participation in better-publicized races, in large part because judges' schedules and ethics code leave them poorly positioned to campaign.
Campaigning in competitive elections, said Kelly Hughes Iverson, co-chair of the Maryland State Bar Association's laws committee, can place judges in ethically compromising positions.
"When the courts are fundraising, the appearance of sitting judges accepting campaign donations from contributors, which includes attorneys and litigants who have cases before them, undermines the public trust in an independent judiciary, and may discourage candidates from applying for the bench at all," Iverson said.
Attorneys are more engaged in judicial elections than the general public, Santini said, and more likely to contribute to a judge's campaign.
Backers also argue that judges, who routinely receive threats from those impacted by their decisions, put their safety at risk when campaigning for reelection.
But not all members of the judiciary are on board with the proposed changes.
"All it does is remove any opportunity for anyone to challenge the person that is named by the governor," said Carroll County Circuit Court Judge Maria Oesterreicher, who won her seat in a 2018 contested election and served on the judicial workgroup that put forward the bill.
Critics like Oesterreicher argue while circuit court elections are imperfect, they are also a rare opportunity for voters to play a larger role in shaping Maryland's judiciary.
If lawmakers are concerned about the qualifications of judicial candidates, she argued, they could require candidates to go through the same vetting process as applicants for appointed seats.
"That's an easy solution, but we've jumped right to the extreme," Oesterreicher said. "I think taking the rights out of the voters' hands is not the right way to fix the problem of judges campaigning if that's the problem that people want to fix."
Skeptics asserted that the appointment process is far from perfect, in large part because it relies on a relatively small group of attorneys to review and recommend candidates. Those attorneys, critics argue, may choose favorites based on politics or personal relationships rather than qualifications.
"It is clubby," said Claudia Barber, who ran unsuccessfully for an Anne Arundel Circuit Court seat last year. "It is also political … which is why, oftentimes, the best is not always chosen."
"I ran against someone who was the third member of the same law firm to be on the bench that only has four seats," Oesterreicher said of her 2018 campaign. The appointment process can favor well-connected attorneys over those with equal or greater qualifications, she argued.
Del. Robin Grammer Jr., a Republican representing Baltimore County, offered harsher criticisms. He argued that the proposal to end contested circuit court elections would primarily benefit the judges, not the public.
"Elections are hard," he told CNS. "You don't get to exempt yourself out of the system and have, frankly, what ends up being a lifetime appointment just because you think it's hard … When is the last time a judge has lost a retention election, like, ever?"
Grammer also contended that judges could avoid ethical concerns about campaign contributions from attorneys by finding alternative fundraising options.
Lawmakers skeptical of eliminating contested circuit court elections have another option this year: expanding voters' input in circuit court primaries.
Del. Chao Wu, a Democrat representing Howard and Montgomery County, is the sponsor of a bill that would replace Maryland's closed partisan primaries for circuit court elections with open, nonpartisan primaries. Closed primaries leave unaffiliated voters — who make up nearly a quarter of the state's electorate — without a voice in key local races, Wu said.
"I think a lot of unaffiliated voters feel they're really disenfranchised," Wu told CNS. "They're not able to vote in (primaries for) one of the most important positions in the state."
Wu's bill received no pushback from members of the House Judiciary Committee, but lawmakers have yet to act on either bill.
If the proposal to end contested circuit court elections passes this session, the question will appear on Maryland voters' ballots in November 2026.

title: Ink Spot: Tattoo Shop Coming to Delaware College Town After Decades-Long Prohibition
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Ink spot: Tattoo shop coming to Delaware college town after decades-long prohibition

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 620

 The city of Newark, which is home to the University of Delaware, soon will be getting its first-ever tattoo shop.On Monday, city council granted a special-use permit to tattoo artist Brittnie Lopez, ending a decades-long prohibition on tattoo shops.
"I'm glad we're on the same page, and it's going to be a fun journey," Lopez said.
Lopez plans to move her business, B13 Tattoos, from Wilmington to a basement storefront at 170 E. Main St., the building that also houses Frolic, Oishii Ocean and Occupy Studio.
She said most of her clients are University of Delaware students, so moving the business to Newark makes sense.
"They can walk to their appointment if they wanted to; they don't have to schedule around their work schedule and get a ride and all that," Lopez said. "I'm trying to just be more convenient for everybody."
A Glasgow High School graduate, Lopez enjoys spending time on Main Street and patronizing the downtown businesses.
"I'm familiar with the area. I love the people," she said. "I mean, you can't beat a college town."
Lopez has been trying to relocate to Newark for several months, but first she needed city council to amend the zoning code.
On Monday, city council added body art establishments — a term that encompasses both tattoo and piercing shops — as an allowable use in certain commercial zoning districts.
Each body art establishment requires a special-use permit, meaning that the business owner needs permission from city council to open a tattoo or piercing shop. The permit can be denied or revoked if council determines that the business would be a detriment to the community.
The law requires that a body art establishment be located at least 300 feet from another body art establishment and at least 200 feet from an elementary, middle or high school.
Another requirement is that body art establishments must operate on an appointment-only basis to avoid the shops turning into a hangout spot and to eliminate spur-of-the-moment tattoo decisions.
Though some council members had expressed reservations about allowing tattoo shops during a previous discussion in November, both the zoning change and Lopez's special-use permit were approved 6-0 on Monday.
Lopez is currently renovating the Main Street shop and hopes to open in March.
She said her business has always operated on an appointment-only basis, which helps her customers feel comfortable. Most of her clients are women, and she works hard to make her shop a safe space.
"The traditional way of a tattoo shop, you walk in there and there's big, muscular men with needles and covered in tattoos, you know, the typical stereotype," she said. "Honestly, we're just girls. We just want something cute, something dainty, something to remember our college years by."
Attitudes toward tattoos are modernizing and for younger generations, they can be a form of therapy, Lopez said.
"I look at it as a meditation, a soothing getaway without booking a flight or getting on a cruise ship,"she said. "It's our mini vacation that we kind of just carry with us wherever we go."
Tattoos are a way of remembering something you're going through, or a way to distract yourself from it, she added.
"It's a different kind of pain, and it's a pain that we pay for, and we keep coming back," Lopez said. "It's kind of crazy, but we love it."
Lopez has been a tattoo artist for seven years.
"I'm covered in tattoos, and that's how I learned, by tattooing myself," she said. "Anything that I can reach on my body, I've tattooed."
Lopez specializes in small tattoos, often floral designs or handwriting.
"It's quick, easy, you're never in my shop longer than an hour, max," she said. "Tattoos are impulsive, and we want a whole bunch of them. So the small ones are easier for people that want a little getaway."

title: Cronan Sworn in as Talbot County Circuit Court Judge

Cronan sworn in as Talbot County Circuit Court judge

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — With hundreds in attendance at the Talbot County Courthouse, Philip Cronan was sworn in as the new judge of the Talbot County Circuit Court Friday afternoon.Cronan, appointed by Gov. Wes Moore last month, assumed the seat from acting Administrative Judge Broughton Earnest. Earnest had been serving since March 2024, when previous Judge Stephen Kehoe was appointed to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
"You can put your stamp on the system of justice here," Earnest said during Friday's ceremony to Cronan. "You're the face of justice, at least in the Circuit Court. There are things you can do not only to perpetuate this system, but to enhance it."
In an interview Friday, Cronan said he's excited to begin as the Circuit Court's administrative judge.
"This is a very humbling experience, and it's just an incredible honor to have the opportunity to serve Talbot County in this capacity," Cronan said. "I look forward to it."
Cronan received his law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law. He served as an assistant state's attorney in Caroline County before beginning his own private practice in Easton.
The new Circuit Court judge is a founding principal of the Easton-based Hollis, Cronan & Fronk law firm. Over the years, his practice has taken a broad path, including domestic litigation, civil litigation, criminal defense and family law.
He said the application and appointment process for the Circuit Court seat was extremely detailed and thorough. Once a judicial nominating commission selected Cronan and two other finalists for the role, they each met with the governor.
It was right before Christmas when Cronan received a call from Moore congratulating him for his appointment.
"I was super excited," Cronan recalled. "I was in court, I was in District Court in Dorchester County when he called. He's such a charismatic, energetic figure, even on the phone. He just makes you feel good."
Cronan says in a one-judge county like Talbot, a judge is "integral" in fairly administering justice.
"I hope to operate in a way that really makes people feel that they are heard, and that they have an opportunity to be heard," Cronan said. "And that they find the process to be fair, even when it doesn't go their way — that they're not steamrolled by the court, so to speak.
"We need to make sure that our citizens find the court a place where they can find justice. If they don't feel heard, if they feel slighted in any way, then we're going to fail. We need to really focus on that."
Cronan previously served as a law clerk for former Talbot County Circuit Court Judge William Horne. He noted Horne held high respect for the institution of the court, something Cronan says was "very powerful."
The longtime Easton attorney aims to channel what he's learned from judges across the state into his work in the Talbot County Circuit Court.
"I've had the benefit of watching so many other judges and how they handle it," Cronan said. "The incredible importance to have a good temperament, to have respect for everybody there, to treat people with dignity."

title: Freedom Caucus Chair Says Officials Who Resist Trump May Pay a Price
author: Paul Kiefer Capital News Service
content:
Freedom Caucus chair says officials who resist Trump may pay a price

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News

 ANNAPOLIS — U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland) said Tuesday he expects President-elect Donald Trump will withhold federal dollars from those who don't comply with mass deportation and other policies — potentially even in Harris' home state of Maryland."After having discussions with incoming members of the Trump administration, they're not going to look favorably upon jurisdictions that, with one hand, ask for federal dollars and, with the other hand, pass it out to illegal immigrants, including protecting them from the reach of federal law, including deportation law," Harris said.
"The fact of the matter is that, when the jurisdiction of Maryland says we're not going to cooperate with deportation policies, why, with the other hand, are they reaching out for federal benefits?" Harris said.
"I think what you're going to see, as part of our efforts to control federal spending," Harris went on, is that "one of the first things we're going to do is go to those jurisdictions that don't cooperate with the federal government and attempt to achieve savings there."
Harris' comments came during a press conference in Annapolis to debut the Maryland House of Delegates' Freedom Caucus, a bloc of half a dozen conservative state delegates modeled after the U.S. House caucus of the same name. Harris, whose district includes Maryland's Eastern Shore, was reelected chair of the House Freedom Caucus last month and is a Trump-friendly member of the House Appropriations Committee.
His prediction on Tuesday echoes similar signals from a handful of Trump's current and former advisers, including Steve Bannon and Newt Gingrich, about suspension of federal funding for jurisdictions that plan not to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. Harris also made similar comments to WBFF-TV Baltimore last week.
Many Democratic officials across the country have expressed concern about mass deportation in their states. But days before Trump is due to be sworn in, most are currently emphasizing their plans to find ways to cooperate with the new president.
Lawmakers in the state's new Freedom Caucus suggested that Harris' ties to the Trump administration could result in the use of federal funding as leverage to boost other state-level priorities. This could potentially give the small group an outsize voice in the General Assembly.
Del. Matt Morgan, a Republican who represents St. Mary's County, is chair of the Maryland General Assembly's Freedom Caucus. At the press conference, he rattled off a list of Republican priorities he hopes will receive a boost from the incoming administration. This would include rolling back some of the General Assembly's recent criminal justice reform efforts, he said.
He also expressed optimism that the Trump administration could shut down the construction of light rail projects that Republicans oppose.
Mass transit projects are draining the transportation trust fund, Morgan said, and "right now they're canceling local projects all across the state for roads and bridges, and overwhelmingly, the people that pay into that fund are motorists."
"We believe there's been a void in conservative leadership in this state for quite some time," Morgan said, "and we're going to fill that void."
The group is small, said Del. Ryan Nawrocki, a Republican from Baltimore County and caucus spokesperson, but that's how the Freedom Caucus in the U.S. House of Representatives got its start.
"You start out with a core group of people that are committed to an ideal," said Nawrocki, "and you demonstrate success, and that's how you grow any group."
Robert Ehrlich, the former Republican governor, also appeared at Monday's press conference, speaking to the assembled crowd alongside members of the group.
"In difficult times, people are challenged, and that means leaders emerge," Ehrlich said, as he stood at the microphone before the news cameras. "Folks behind me are clearly leaders that are emerging in Maryland today."
The new caucus's model is to "equip conservatives to win on issues across the country," according to Rachel Ullmann, communications and community outreach director for the legislature's District 7 delegates.
"We stand firmly with the National Network's policy of 'fighting federal overreach and standing firm against those in both parties who prioritize seizing political power over representing constituents,'" she wrote in an email to Capital News Service.
Maryland's Freedom Caucus has not yet sought formal recognition from their party's House and Senate chamber leaders, Nawrocki told reporters.
"There's a possibility that we might do so," Nawrocki said. House Minority Leader Del. Jason Buckel, a Republican representing Allegany County, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Maryland Legislators Kick Off 447th General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
Maryland legislators kick off 447th General Assembly

 January 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 ANNAPOLIS — With snow piled up around the Statehouse, Maryland lawmakers returned to downtown Annapolis for the 447th General Assembly on Wednesday.More than 560 bills were prefiled in either the House of Delegates or Senate prior to the opening session. While both chambers began introducing bills Wednesday, the focus largely remained on the state's looming budget deficit that will be tackled in the coming weeks.
The state is predicted to face a $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026. Gov. Wes Moore (D), who some Republicans have criticized for his fiscal decisions, must submit his balanced budget proposal by next Wednesday.
Leadership in the House and Senate acknowledged the deficit will be center stage but spoke optimistically about what's ahead.
House Speaker Adrienne Jones, a Democrat from Baltimore County, said the House, which reviews the budget first, will "use it to reflect our values."
"As we begin this session, I know there has been a lot of talk about our financial limitations. And there should be," Jones said. "We can't deny our difficult fiscal reality. But instead of talking about what our budget can't do, I'd like to talk about what it can do. Most importantly, our budget has the power to protect the most vulnerable Marylanders."
Jones noted health care and transportation as areas that will continue to be prioritized, as well as the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's expansive education initiative.
"We don't want to talk about cuts and prioritizing programs, but we have to," Jones said. "We don't want to talk about high-energy costs, but we have to. And we have to talk about protecting the investment we made for our students and teachers in The Blueprint."
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Baltimore Democrat beginning his sixth year in the role, said the General Assembly's efforts to fund and facilitate reconstruction of the Francis Scott Key Bridge last year showed the aptitude of Maryland's lawmakers.
"This institution showed exactly who it is," Ferguson said. "Within days, we had put together legislation working with our House counterparts, with the governor, setting up the PORT Act in a bipartisan way to find ways to put resources immediately to use, to set the state up for success in the midst of crisis."
Ferguson said the budget deficit is the General Assembly's next significant challenge.
"I've been thinking about it a little bit differently recently, in that yes it is a challenge, but really, it's an opportunity for us in this body," Ferguson said. " … What do we want our future to look like? How do we take this challenge and have the hard conversations about what do we prioritize to invest in people and to build communities in a way that everyone has the opportunity to thrive."
The Senate president offered positivity through the fact that the state came in under budget and ahead of schedule on a significant project just outside of the Statehouse — the Maryland Department of Legislative Services building. A ribbon-cutting ceremony will be held tomorrow, he said.
"What emerged was everything that the state of Maryland should look like," Ferguson said of the new building that he called "beautiful."
Leadership in both chambers remained the same Wednesday. Ferguson and Senate President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine, a Democrat from Prince George's County, were unanimously nominated to their positions.
In the House, Speaker Pro Tem Dana Stein, a Baltimore County Democrat, was nominated and approved for a second consecutive year. Jones begins her sixth full term as speaker.
On Wednesday, the House Speaker reflected on the fact that her first job in public service was made possible by the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act, legislation the late President Jimmy Carter extended during his time in office.
"I know that we all love public service," Jones said. "And when I think about public service, I think about the late President Jimmy Carter. As it turns out, I owe a lot to President Carter."
Jones said those are the ways in which "government can do powerful things for regular people."
"Progress isn't linear, it's incremental," Jones said. "It takes time. It takes resilience."

Service dog group names pup after late veterans affairs secretary

 December 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News

 Not every hero needs a bronze statue or a painted portrait hanging in a prominent building to be remembered. Sometimes a dog will do just fine.Earlier this year, an organization called Warrior Canine Connection announced it was naming a service dog after George Owings III.
Owings, a Calvert County resident, Vietnam veteran, Marine and former secretary of Maryland's Department of Veterans Affairs, died Oct. 31, 2023.
In February 2020, under Owings' leadership the Maryland Veterans Service Animal Program bestowed on Warrior Canine Connection $30,000 in funding to help support the placement of service dogs with wounded armed forces veterans.
The Montgomery County-based organization's leadership was pleased with the allocation.
"It's no secret that service dogs are an amazing tool to help in the veteran recovery process and by making them more available, together, we can help serve more of our nation's heroes," Rick Yount, the founder and executive director of Warrior Canine Connection, said at the time.
"For our veterans who have honorably served in the military and who have also given so much to our state and nation, this is but one way we can give back," Owings remarked after the $30,000 in funding was presented to Warrior Canine Connection in 2020.
The impetus for that bestowal was launched three years earlier when an Anne Arundel County state lawmaker, Sen. Bryan W. Simonaire (R), sponsored a bill that, when passed, established the Maryland Service Animal Program.
Josh Marks, a Carroll County resident who is a veterans advocate, nominated Owings this year to have a service dog named in his honor.
"George was an honorable man," Marks said. "Honor is simply the morality of superior men. What better legacy to leave?"
The connection's announcement that a fledgling service dog would be named "Owings," recounts the actions of U.S. Marine Sgt. George W. Owings III during his four years of service during the Vietnam War.
The citation noted Owings earned the Navy and Marine Corps Medal "for heroism in rescuing the crew of an OH-23 helicopter on the evening of Aug. 3, 1967. Upon observing the helicopter crash approximately 200 yards off the beach at Marine Corps Air Station Chu Lai Republic of Vietnam, Sgt. Owings took immediate action to assist downed crew members. He, along with other marines, immediately ran to a 750 pound fiberglass boat positioned 50 yards from the water, which could obviously be used in a rescue attempt. Sgt. Owings and the other marines began struggling with the heavy boat to launch it into the water."
Despite the challenging waters, Owings and other marines were able to subsequently save three injured crewmen from the downed chopper, guiding the vessel back to shore so the survivors could receive medical attention.
In addition to the Navy and Marine Corps Medal, Owings received a Presidential Unit Citation, a Navy Unit Commendation with Bronze Star Badge and the Vietnam Service Medal with Silver Star Badge.
Owings, the service canine, was raised by a Germantown couple and as of this writing, remains in training.

 Cecil County organizers partnered with gas station chain Sheetz helped facilitate deliveries of holiday wreathes to various cemeteries in Cecil County, including Rosebank and St. Mary Anne's, last week to be used in Wreaths Across America across the county. Wreaths Across America is an annual tribute to our nation's veterans, honoring those who served by placing a wreath on their graves around the holidays.Julia Swoboda initiated the first Wreaths Across America event in Cecil County nine years ago at St. Mary Anne's, after she attended the annual Arlington National Cemetery wreath ceremony in 2016 — where the initiative first began in 1992, and where nearly 400,000 veterans and their families are buried.
"After that, I was really inspired to come back to Cecil County and start our event," Swoboda said. "I think anyone who's done that [gone to Arlington's ceremony] really understands the impact that makes on you and then just inspires you really to see what you can do in your community."

 CAMBRIDGE — The state of the state's budget took up a large part of the conversation at a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon with state legislators on Dec. 4.The Lower Shore delegation answered questions from chamber members regarding concerns about Maryland's fiscal health, with a looming $2.7 billion state budget deficit predicted in fiscal year 2026.
"The reality is that if you continue to do the things that have gotten us into this deficit, it's only going to take us back there again," Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "There needs to be a structural, fundamental change."
Mautz and Dels. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke at the chamber lunch. They, along with the rest of the state's legislators, will head back to Annapolis in January for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.
In talking about the state's budget, Mautz also said there should be incentives in place to try to drive state agencies to save money.
Sample-Hughes said the state should do its fiscal homework and find out what it "really (has) to work with."
"But I do believe that we can still address and attack some of these goals that we have, whether it's education, whether it's climate, whether it's criminal justice," she said. "We can do it in a pragmatic way."
Adams said to solve the budget problem, the state has to leverage and grow its private sector.
"You do not do what we've done for the past two years," he said. He said the state and its leadership need to stop spending so much, own up to the problem and stop blaming it on COVID-19.
Hutchinson expressed his concerns with the transportation budget and the lack of funding for many infrastructure projects across the state.
"We've got to pay attention to our transportation budget," he said.
BLUEPRINTThe legislators also talked about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over a 10-year period.
Sample-Hughes said although Blueprint's goals are important, the General Assembly's decision to pass the plan has contributed to the state's budget deficit. She later advocated for giving more resources to the nonprofits that already serve 3 and 4 year olds, rather than putting money toward expanding early childhood education in the state's public school systems.
Mautz said he thinks the project needs to be paused so that the plan's strengths and weaknesses can be better evaluated.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe legislators also talked about the state of juvenile crime in Maryland, with Sample-Hughes calling for the removal of Department of Juvenile Services Secretary Vincent Schiraldi.
Hutchinson said that with recent juvenile justice reforms going into effect Nov. 1, he doesn't think a lot of legislators are going to want to discuss juvenile crime this upcoming session.
"Because they'll say, 'We just put that in place. We haven't even been able to see the results,'" he said.
Adams said law enforcement is needed now more than ever and officers need to be able to do their jobs.
"If you want a society, if you want a City of Cambridge, if you want an Eastern Shore (or) State of Maryland, if you want a United States that is civil, there have to be consequences," he said.

 EASTON — Local leaders and officials thanked Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.) for his service to the Eastern Shore on Friday morning as the 81-year-old nears his final days of his 18th year in the U.S. Senate.In his farewell tour to the Eastern Shore, the longtime congressman made a stop at the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy to speak with local representatives, including Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan.
These officials and state legislators, including Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), thanked Cardin for his professionalism, ability to work across the political aisle and commitments to the Eastern Shore.
In September, Cardin and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced $10.6 million in federal funding for Chesapeake Bay restoration, $2.8 million of which went to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy. On Friday, Mautz emphasized Cardin's success in providing money to maintain the shoreline.
"At a critical juncture where we are in the world and all the things that are happening, Sen. Cardin is a force in Washington," Mautz said.
"I'm going to miss you," Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "The one thing I respect (about) you most is that you're going out on top. I see a lot of politicians who don't know when to step down."
Revisiting his top initiatives throughout his three terms in the Senate, Cardin noted the work done at Capitol Hill to improve Maryland colleges and universities, expand healthcare on the Shore and upgrade water infrastructure.
"There's so much competition for clean water and wastewater facilities that sometimes rural areas don't get their fair share," Cardin said. "We're able to work together to make sure you get your fair share under the revolving funds, but also then use our earmarks for where gaps have taken place."
Cardin said local leadership on the Shore is as impressive as it gets across the state, and he thanked local councils for ensuring rural areas achieve a balance of having an economic future and maintaining a sense of uniqueness.
Cardin spoke highly of Easton — a town he says is attracting much attention in the nation's capital. The senator added that officials in Talbot County are adequately serving all people.
"You also have challenges, hunger and low-income families," Cardin told members of the Talbot County Council. "And you're taking steps to deal with those issues as well, so we appreciate that. … There is diversity here. And you have helped deal with preserving dignity for all of the people in the county."
PASSING THE TORCHCardin opted not to run for reelection, leaving an open seat in the Senate that will be filled by Democrat Angela Alsobrooks, who defeated Republican opponent and former Gov. Larry Hogan in November's election.
Having worked with Alsobrooks, the Prince George's County executive, Cardin said he's confident in Maryland's newest senator.
"We've had several conversations," Cardin said in an interview. "I think she understands the responsibilities, so she has the whole package. I think she'll do a great job."
Cardin emphasized that former Sen. Barbara Mikulski (D-Md.), a mentor of his who he served alongside in the Senate from 2007 to 2017, taught him the tradition of Maryland's delegation working together instead of separately. He hopes Van Hollen and Alsobrooks carry that torch beginning in January.
"I think that tradition will continue, no doubt about it," Cardin said. "Sen. Alsobrooks will continue to be not only an incredible leader, but also part of a great team."

 Newark, Delaware's decades-long prohibition on tattoo and piercing shops may be coming to an end.A majority of city council members indicated earlier this month they would be in favor of allowing such businesses to open. A formal vote will be taken later.
The discussion was initiated by a request from Brittnie Lopez, the owner of B13 Tattoos, currently located on Miller Road in Wilmington.
After operating the shop for three years, Lopez wants to move it to Newark's Main Street, noting that many of her customers are down here. B13 Tattoos operates on an appointment-only basis, and Lopez is the only employee.
"As the City of Newark has continued to thrive and add new additions and create different opportunities, I think that this would be perfect for the center of Newark," Lopez told council members.
She is in negotiations to lease a vacant storefront at 170 E. Main St, the building that also houses Frolic, Oishii Sushi & Ramen and Occupy Studio.
"I recently found out you guys have no tattoo parlors in the City of Newark, and I would love to be first," Lopez said.
In order for her to do so, however, city council must add body art establishments — a term that encompasses both tattoo and piercing shops — to the zoning code. Currently, body art establishments are not listed as an allowable use in any of the zoning districts, meaning they are essentially banned from opening anywhere in city limits.
This is not the first time Newark has discussed legalizing body art establishments.
In 2016, a business owner wanted to open a piercing shop on Main Street, but he ultimately dropped his request before it came to city council for a vote.
The topic came up again in 2022 when councilmen Travis McDermott and Jason Lawhorn said they had heard from people who wanted to open tattoo shops in the city. Council directed staffers to research the issue, but it fell by the wayside amidst other priorities and was never formally considered.
Lawhorn said tattoos and the people who have them were once stereotyped, but he argued that times have changed.
"Maybe in the '50s or '60s, it seems like it was associated with biker clubs and prostitution and things like that," he said. "It has evolved well past that."
Lawhorn, who said he has four tattoos himself, cited statistics that show that more than 40 percent of adults under 50 have a tattoo.
Allowing tattoo shops will bring something new to downtown Newark, he said.
"I think it adds some flavor and some culture to the city," Lawhorn said. "We love our restaurants, but there's not a lot of grit to Main Street."
Councilwoman Dwendolyn Creecy noted that tattooing goes back centuries and is important in many cultures.
"I don't have a problem with this. Not one," Creecy said.
The only council members opposed were Corinth Ford and John Suchanec.
"I really don't think that this is a business that would be compatible or required on Main Street," Suchanec said. "I probably have to come up with 1,000 reasons why I'm taking this position, other than my personal preference not to have tattoo parlors on Main Street."
He also worried that University of Delaware students would upset their parents by getting tattoos.
"One big, big concern is students going home and showing off their tattoos," Suchanec said, speculating their parents would respond by saying, "you didn't ask my permission."
Ford said her concerns are about safety and sanitation.
"I really do not want this kind of business on Main Street," she said.
The planning department will now work on language to add body art establishments to the zoning code.
It's expected that the law will require a special-use permit, meaning that each business owner will need permission from city council to open a tattoo or piercing shop. The permit can be denied or revoked if council determines that the business would be a detriment to the community. The city is also considering requiring body art establishments to operate on an appointment-only basis to eliminate spur-of-the-moment tattoo decisions.
The planning commission will vote on the law Dec. 3, with a final vote by city council in February.

 CAMBRIDGE — Serving in the U.S. Army gave Gov. Wes Moore (D) the chance to see parts of the country and world he never knew existed.The experience also gave him the opportunity to create lasting bonds with people different from him.
"I can tell you that some of my best friends on this planet are people who society tells me I shouldn't even be talking to," he said during a Veterans Day breakfast at American Legion Post 91 in Cambridge. "And these are my brothers now. And my sisters."
Before shaking hands with Maryland veterans and serving them breakfast, Moore — who was deployed to Afghanistan in 2005 — talked about the military's ability to unite people and the importance of unity in a time of division.
"I could not tell you the political affiliation of people that I served with," he said. "Because we didn't talk about it. ... Because it didn't matter. We fought for each other."

There is a lot society can learn from veterans, he said.
"This Veterans Day, I think it becomes incredibly important that we hold those values dear and that we understand that even in the darkest moments, that it's faith that is what's going to drive us through," he said.
In his speech, Moore also talked about Maryland's efforts to support veterans. He mentioned tax relief for veterans as well as the Time to Serve Act, which extends military leave for state employees who serve in the National Guard or Reserve.
Along with Moore, American Legion Department of Maryland Commander David Heredia and Maryland Secretary of Veterans and Military Families Anthony Woods spoke at the breakfast event that drew an array of American Legion members from different posts.

Steve Williams, who served in the U.S. Air Force from 1964 to 1968, said medical care and homelessness are two of the most important issues when it comes to supporting veterans. He said he thinks Moore is "pretty well on top of" what the issues affecting veterans are because Moore is a veteran.

According to Feehley, spending even an hour with veterans could provide essential socialization to the many men and women who spent their time serving the country.
"Socialization is just a great part of life, and they don't get an opportunity to socialize too much," Feehley said. "So I give an hour a day every now and then. For me it's giving back. It's giving back for what they gave to me and to you and everybody else."
The members of the Veteran Affairs Committee shared their different reasons for joining the military, and as they opened up, more veterans began sharing their experiences.
For one of the veterans in the facility, the Air Force provided him the opportunity to go to college. As the eldest of six, economically it would not have been possible otherwise, but through signing up for the service he said he was able to grow into the man he became.
Another man said he was one of the first Black men to be invited to the Gold Naval Academy in Annapolis. He said it was a sign of progress, since months before Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
Chivy Wieland, a member of the Veteran Affairs Committee, shared stories of his time in basic training and the hardships he and other recruits endured.
Wieland said, drill sergeants that molded the new recruits did so with purpose.
"They will tear you down, so they can build you back up, and then you'll be ready to fight and you'll be somebody that you're supposed to be," Wieland said.
Mike Hare, a Navy veteran, said he spent time in Spain while in service. During his time there, he tried Ouzo, a spirit made from grape must, for the first time and proudly bought his first leather jacket to impress local women.
Over the course of the morning, the veterans laughed, shared stories, jokes and concerns for the future of the military as it continues to change. Feehley said these social actions allow veterans to feel personally enriched and it is good to recognize the sacrifices made by veterans.
"We have a good time because it's veterans helping veterans," he said.

 EASTON — A resident of Easton Club East has filed a complaint requesting an injunction against the Easton Club East Community Association's board election after his candidacy was rejected.Jerome Wade, represented by attorney Lyndsey Ryan, filed the complaint on Oct. 21, according to Talbot County Circuit Court records. It outlines why he is "challenging the unlawful rejection of his nomination" and his claims that the association exceeded its authority and violated its bylaws.
Easton Club East, a single-family home neighborhood located off of Dutchmans Lane, is home to more than 800 residents, according to its website. Its Board of Directors, made up of three to seven members, sought nomination forms for three expiring positions on Sept. 16, according to the complaint.

title: On the Ballot: What Is Question 1 or the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment?
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
On the ballot: What is Question 1 or the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment?

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 565
