 ANNAPOLIS. When more than 200 rural community leaders and other stakeholders came together for the Rural Maryland Council's recent Pathways to Prosperity summit, there was one clear message. rural communities have an inherent ability to pivot, respond and recover during hard times.The breakout sessions focused on this ability to dig deep and come up with creative solutions, a quality that rural communities can share with its suburban and urban counterparts so that all of Maryland can tackle the tough issues and come out the other end more resilient and sustainable, the council said in a press release.
"Housing is an economic development issue," said Andy Bauer, vice president and Baltimore Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, during the lunch plenary. "The housing issue is something that's going to be with us for a while. It's going to take a lot of innovation in order to provide or make it easier for more supply to come online in either the form of greater density and more single family units." "It's going to have to be intentional," he added. "At the end of the day everybody in those communities are going to have to be onboard." Finding balance and leveraging challenges for the better was the message that Maryland Secretary of Agriculture Kevin Atticks delivered to summit attendees.
"Agriculture has to be profitable," he said. "Our farmers and our agricultural land are under so much pressure from development and from our clean energy goals." He didn't stop there, adding a message about resource conservation.
"We are farming in the context of the Bay. That's a pressure. We need to protect the land, preserve the land, and make sure the land is working for the Bay, not just being profitable," he said.
The summit closed with a message of hope and encouragement to tackle the challenges that lie ahead and to continue to break barriers from Maryland's first woman comptroller Brooke Lierman.
"We are focused on a new vision under our new leadership, and that is to be a partner in creating a state that is more equitable, more resilient and more prosperous so that every Marylander can reach their full potential," Lierman said. "There are still barriers to break, but by working together we can keep breaking them." The summit was just one of the key accomplishments for the Rural Maryland Council this year, the press release said. The Council received historic funding of the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund in the amount $9,050,000, along with the Maryland Agricultural Education and Rural Development Assistance Fund (MAERDAF), which received an additional $118,485. The funding enabled RMC to provide grants to the state's five rural regional councils as well as 84 RMPIF grants totaling $8,369,629 and 47 MAERDAF grants totaling $1,153,203.
Other 2023 RMC achievements include monitoring 135 bills, writing 60 position statements, passing three bills and hosting seven legislative committee meetings as well as co-hosting the 2023 Regional Rural Broadband Forum with the USDA Rural Development on June 21.
Looking to the coming year's legislative session, RMC has established several key priorities including: ¡ Level funding of $9 million in the fiscal year 2025 operating budget for Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund.
¡ Efforts to address affordable housing issues such as efforts to repair and weatherize homes to keep seniors aging in their homes as well as the creation of additional workforce housing units to serve public service and moderate income workers.
¡ $1,000,000 for the Wood Products Industry Equity Investment Fund to reach renewable energy goals and support upgrades in electric infrastructure.
¡ Establishing programs and policies to sustain and enhance agricultural production and agri-tourism and efforts to address food security.
"As we close this year, we'll take a moment to appreciate our successes, and then quickly roll up our sleeves as we know that the challenges facing our rural communities continue to be numerous and complex," RMC Chair Susan O'Neill said. "We encourage all our stakeholders to join us and draw on their resilience and ability to innovate so together we can build a stronger future for all Marylanders." Founded in 1994, the Rural Maryland Council operates under the direction of a 40-member executive board in a nonpartisan and nondiscriminatory manner.
For more information on the Rural Maryland Council or to get involved, visit rural. maryland.gov or contact RMC at 410-841-5772 or rmc.mda@maryland.gov.

title: Maryland Transportation Chief Proposes $3.3B in Budget Cuts
content:
Maryland transportation chief proposes $3.3B in budget cuts

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 752

 ANNAPOLIS - Gov. Wes Moore's administration is proposing roughly $3.3 billion in wide-ranging cuts for the state's six-year transportation spending plan, which is facing inflationary pressures as traditional revenue sources haven't kept up with costs, the state's transportation secretary said Tuesday.The proposal, which could be adjusted by the General Assembly next year, will have an impact on highways and transit service, as well as other transportation spending.The approach includes about $1 billion in reductions in the transportation department's operating budget, $2 billion from the capital program and about $400 million in grant reductions to local governments, the department said in a news release Tuesday."We're trying to pull as many levers as we can to make this as painless as we can," Paul Wiedefeld, Maryland's transportation secretary, told The Associated Press in an interview.The proposal is part of a larger budget challenge the state is facing. Moore, a Democrat, and the legislature, which is controlled by Democrats, are grappling with projected future budget deficits in the state's operating budget, which is separate from the transportation spending plan.Moore put officials on notice in August that tough budget decisions were coming, during a speech at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference.When state lawmakers convene for their annual legislative session in January, they will be working to balance the budget for the next fiscal year with an estimated shortfall of about $400 million.They also are facing rising budget gapsin future years, as the state continues to implement an education funding reform law with phased-in funding.One of the biggest cuts in the transportation funding plan would be to major highway and transit expansion projects that are not advertised by Jan. 1. Those construction dollars would be moved out beyond fiscal year 2029, Wiedefeld said.The plan also would cut funds for maintenance projects by 30%. For highways, that reduction would affect day-to-day operations such as mowing lawns, picking up litter and fixing potholes."They're still going to be doing them, but not at the degree that we would prefer," Wiedefeld said.The plan also calls for saving roughly $40 million a year by shutting down smaller branch offices for the MVA and reducing office hours. The plan also includes increasing airport parking fees.Wiedefeld said the state will maintain matching money to receive federal funding. The transportation department said federal investments add up to about $7 billion."We're not going to leave any money on the table because you're getting roughly 80 cents on the dollar," Wiedefeld said.U.S. Rep. David Trone, a Democrat who represents western Maryland and parts of Montgomery County in the suburbs of the nation's capital, criticized the plan for using funds in the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to backfill the department's budget. In a letter to Wiedefeld, Trone wrote that the plan would re-allocate funds from 12 of 33 approved priority roadway projects, reduce transit services and cut maintenance projects."These projects were a huge win and Marylanders were excited to see these long-awaited investments being made in their communities, as well as the thousands of good-paying jobs that would come with them," Trone wrote.The proposal retains project development funds for Baltimore's Red Line, Southern Maryland Rapid Transit, the Frederick Douglass Tunnel Project, the replacement American Legion Bridge and other key projects, the transportation department said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.The secretary, a former general manager and CEO of Metro, said Maryland won't back away from investments needed to support the subway system linking Maryland and Virginia with the District of Columbia.The funding crunch comes as revenue sources have not kept up with operating costs, Wiedefeld said. Operating costs have risen roughly 7% annually, while revenues have gone up only about 1%, he said.The state's vehicle titling tax isn't keeping up with costs, as more people keep their vehicles longer, and the gas tax also doesn't keep pace because of increasing efficiency and electric car use. Wiedefeld also noted that transit ridership has not bounced back to what it was before the COVID-19 pandemic.The secretary also pointed out that the state has hit a debt-limit cap, creating another challenge for capital needs.

'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays

 ST. MICHAELS - A small line formed outside of the St. Michaels Community Center's temporary location on Talbot Street in the late afternoon on Monday.While some people waited to pick up their usual grocery items from the food pantry, others came for a hefty frozen turkey, pie, a sack of potatoes and a large bag of canned and dry items - all the fixings for a delicious and plentiful Thanksgiving dinner.Food Bank Director Amy DeWitt said that the SMCC has been handing out these "Thanksgiving boxes" to people who might not be able to afford a full Thanksgiving dinner for at least six years."(With) the cost of food nowadays, I think a lot of people just can't afford to go out and buy a turkey," DeWitt said. "And I think it's very important for them to have a meal they can prepare at home for their family." From 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. on Monday, DeWitt and her small team handed out all the turkey day classics for residents to cook on Thursday."The boxes are like an addition to what they already have at home," Mark Singleton, DeWitt's assistant, said."So just to push things along, maybe even press the meal for another day or two." In addition to the Thanksgiving boxes, the SMCC is hosting an eat-in community dinner on Wednesday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome. Those in attendance will be served turkey and gravy from Ava's Pizzeria and Wine Bar as well as cornbread stuffing, garlic mashed red skin potatoes, green bean casserole, dinner rolls and homemade apple and pumpkin pies.DeWitt estimated that they will serve between 150 and 175 prepared meals on Wednesday. Kerri Clear, executive chef at the SMCC, who is making most of the dishes for Wednesday's community dinner, said the community is very supportive of what the community center does to help residents."We get a lot of donations," Clear said, "a lot of interest from the community." DeWitt said that all of her clients are "very thankful" for the special holiday meals that the SMCC hands out.Singleton said each person appreciates what they do."They show us every time they come in," he said."They're really thankful." And Dewitt, Clear and Singleton are just happy to help out in the community."We just want to feed 'em," DeWitt Said.

 With no comment from the public during a hearing or remarks from the town council during an Oct. 19 monthly meeting, the town ofChes-apeake Beach unanimously passed an ordinance addressing legal cannabis.The new law prohibits the smoking or ingesting of cannabis in several public areas, including town hall, Veterans Park, Bayfront Park, Kellam's Field, boardwalk and town pocket parks. Additionally, the ban includes public areas at local businesses.The ordinance was discussed during the mayor and council's September work session, with it then being introduced during that month's council meeting.Acting upon Maryland voters' approval by referendum of the legalization of recreational marijuana for adults 21 or older, the Maryland General Assembly passed the accompanying Cannabis Reform Act earlier this year."Because I'm a nerd, I probably read that 100-page bill 20 or 30 times," Chesapeake Beach Mayor Patrick "Irish" Mahoney declared during the September work session.After familiarizing himself with the new law, Mahoney told the council he has testified before a state Senate committee and worked with other mayors through the Maryland Municipal League to find ways to comply without ceding total control."Just common sense," Councilwoman Valerie Beaudin said of the ordinance draft. "It falls along the lines ofwhat's already in place" for smoking and vaping tobacco and drinking alcohol.Councilman Charlie Fink said he wanted assurances the ordinance wouldn't result in people "being stopped and frisked.""If you have it in your pocket, that's fine,"Todd Pounds, town attorney, stated.During that same work session the mayor and council discussed a second cannabis-related ordinance affecting the legal sale of the substance within the town limits.Mahoney noted that unlike many other states, Maryland lawmakers declined to consider a "local opt out" for state jurisdictions that don't wish to have cannabis sales within their confines."You're trying to create a wholesome environment," Mahoney said of a prohibition on cannabis sales.The mayor added that the way the state is planning to tax the newly legalized product and distribute receipts to jurisdictions would mean the town would receive "basically nothing."A public hearing on the latter ordinance proposal did not happen at the October meeting.When asked late last week why there was no hearing for the other proposed ordinance, Mahoney told Southern Maryland News that he learned at a Maryland Municipal League meeting recently that the state legislature is planning to revisit the law next session to clear up some of its ambiguous aspects.

title: 'It's going to carry us into the future' - U.S. Constitution celebrated at Talbot County Courthouse

content:
'It's going to carry us into the future' - U.S. Constitution celebrated at Talbot County Courthouse

 EASTON - The Star-Spangled Banner, performed by 35 students from Easton Middle School, resounded in the area surrounding the Talbot County Courthouse Saturday, Sept. 16.The band's rendition of the national anthem kicked off the second annual Constitution Day celebration in Easton. A crowd gathered to listen to speeches, enjoy Rita's Italian Ice and learn more about the Constitution of the United States.The event was hosted by the Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance.Along with speeches from an array of people - from elected officials to students - actor Darius Wallace performed a re-enactment of Frederick Douglass speaking about freedom and the Constitution.Wallace received a standing ovation for his performance.Easton resident John Miller was especially impressed with Wallace's performance."That took great appreciation of our freedoms and made us aware of how important our freedoms were and what slavery means and that there is still work to do," Miller said.Miller said it's important that the Constitution is still acknowledged today because it's "where our government gets its power." Speakers at the event, who talked about the importance of the Constitution, included Maryland State Sen. Johnny Mautz; Tarence Bailey Sr., founder and president of The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation; Joseph Prud'Homme, a professor in Religion, Politics, and Culture at Washington College; Zach Affeldt, a student at Washington College; William Fachet, a student at University of Maryland College Park; Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Ron James, a Veterans of Foreign Wars member.Mautz talked about his experience delving into the Constitution at law school."Never did I think that the Constitution was fun or exciting until you start to talk about free speech," he said. "And then we're into the good stuff." Mautz said that without free speech protections in the Constitution, we wouldn't be standing here today.Bailey spoke about the Constitution being important for everyday life during his speech."I think it's very important, especially for youth, that they learn the Constitution, know what's in it and know what applies to them," he said.Michelle Ewing, co-director of the Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance, said the mission of the organization is to educate the public and raise awareness about the U.S Constitution. She said the group offers scholarships to graduating seniors and non-traditional students who want to go back to school."We want to get the youth involved and informed," she said.At the end of his speech, Mautz talked about the importance of the Constitution today."We have to go back to the Constitution and use the Constitution to fix the problems, not tear it apart," he said. "It's gotten us to where we are. It is going to carry us into the future."

 EASTON - The Talbot County 100+ Women Who Care group started off strong at its inaugural meeting Monday evening, which ended on a high note with a $13,000 donation to the Talbot Interfaith Shelter.Living up to the group's name, over 100 women gathered at the Talbot County Free Library to hear quick presentations from three local nonprofits seeking funding.At Monday's meeting, the first three nominees - the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Foundation, Talbot Humane and Talbot Interfaith Shelter - shared presentations and stories on why the $13,000 contribution from group members should be awarded to them and how each would use the funds.Each nonprofit was given five minutes to present, followed by several minutes of questions from attendees looking to make informed decisions.Audience members then filled out voting forms, casting their ballots for the nonprofit they found to be the most compelling.Following a quick tally, Talbot Interfaith Shelter was selected as the first awardee.Founded in 2008, TIS is dedicated to ending homelessness in the Mid-Shore region by providing shelter, stability, support and success to families and individuals in need, said Julie Lowe, the shelter's executive director.But TIS has expanded since then, she added - the shelter now offers education on money management, the root causes of poverty, accessing resources and weaning off those resources."That is when I see the joy in people's faces, when they say 'I don't need that CarePack anymore on the weekends for my kids, I don't need that temporary cash assistance anymore, I have a job and I'm able to provide for my family," Lowe said.However, the cost of childcare remains a significant struggle."The expense of childcare is hard for people with a really good job to manage, much less somebody who's in a homeless shelter trying to find a job, even a minimum wage job, to support their family and be able to get them back into housing," Lowe said.Laura Richeson, TIS' director of development and marketing, said the nonprofit has a $1.3 million operating budget this year, a daunting but fulfilling goal to fundraise for. Finding money to subsidize childcare costs for working parents in the shelter is the "biggest issue." After selecting Monday's awardee, the philanthropic group of women also submitted nominations for the next meeting's presenters.The group's next meeting, slated for sometime in January, will feature presentations from the St. Michaels Fire Department, CarePacks of Talbot County and the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Cancer Foundation, which will be back for a second time.community members who committed to contributing were happy with how the group's inaugural meeting turned out.{p dir="ltr"}Vivian Landau of St. Michaels said she's always been involved with philanthropic events, so the local 100+ Women Who Care group starting up seemed "perfect" for her to join.For Colleen Kennedy of Bozman, making contributions to places she cares about isn't new. She's donated to a scholarship fund at the high school she attended, but the 100+ Women Who Care group in Talbot County has a key difference."I liked that I can actually pick and see where the money goes," she said.The Talbot County group's founding members - Amanda David, Karen Gadson and Michele Lowe - were also pleased with the turnout and excitement for the group's first meeting."It's a very simple and effective way to impact all of the (Talbot County) nonprofits who are in the trenches, making our community a better place," David said of the organization's goal.

title: I Don't Come From Political Lineage
author: Kiersten Hacker; Capital News Service
content:
I don't come from political lineage

 September 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Kiersten Hacker; Capital News Service | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 600
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON - Gov. Wes Moore fended off questions Tuesday on whether he'll run in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary during an interview with global news organization Semafor, saying he had no interest in higher office and turning the subject to his nontraditional political background."I think it's really important for people to remember that I am probably the most improbable governor in this country," Moore said in answer to the first question from Semafor cofounder and Editor-at-large Steve Clemons. "I'm a person who has never come from a political lineage." Moore, an author, nonprofit executive and former Army officer, had not held political office before winning the governor's election in 2022.Moore turned his focus to Maryland, discussing plans to revive the state's economy through targeted investments in its assets and better serve constituents with a data-driven approach to policy changes.Moore often defines Maryland as "asset-rich and strategy-poor," and cites the contrast presented by the state's high concentration of prominent institutions of higher education, military facilities and government agencies, such as the National Security Agency, with its sluggish economic growth rate of.2% in the past 4 years. The current economic strategy of spreading funding across numerous projects "doesn't make sense," he said, explaining he'll use a more focused approach.In June, Moore established the Maryland Economic Council, charging it with creating economic recommendations by the next legislative session in January. After the General Assembly passed numerous measures to affect systemic budgetary changes during the last session, a report from the Department of Legislative Services predicted a $418 million structural deficit for fiscal year 2025.Moore said his administration will use data to drive policy decisions, especially when looking to minimize socioeconomic disparities, and he used environmental injustice in Baltimore as an example."You can't understand what these disparities look like if we aren't able to fully appreciate the measure of intentionality that very much existed in the creation of that and the lack of intentionality when it comes to how we're going to address it." The administration must consider the root causes of poverty, investing in transit, the public education system and programs to combat the teacher shortage, Moore said, to jumpstart economic growth.Creating new opportunities for young people to succeed in different areas will help fight juvenile crime and keep violence out of communities, Moore said. Using data and technology in innovative ways can also help ensure that solutions to crime are predictive rather than reactive.Increasing public safety is his top priority, Moore said, highlighting the need for "appropriate intensity, absolute integrity, and full accountability" in the policing system as well as a need for crisis intervention teams to shift the response of mental health calls away from police officers. Over $100 million was invested directly in behavioral health, Moore said.Moore noted that police officers respond to all situations, and many times they are met with circumstances they cannot fix.He called for change, saying that public safety is in part a matter of creating a better livelihood for people.Moore said his administration invested $122 million in local law enforcement, $17.5 million of which went to Baltimore City, where the police department has been under a federal agreement to make reforms since 2016.Moore also invested in intelligence sharing through the Maryland Coordination and Analysis Center and organized crime units.In Baltimore, other reform means combating gun trafficking, filling the police shortage with well-trained officers, and developing more intentional solutions, said Moore, who places special importance on these issues as a Baltimore native."I love my state, all 24 jurisdictions. But I'm a Baltimorean," Moore said."That's who I am. Can't understand me if you don't understand Baltimore."
